papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess the value of genetic testing in the prenatal congenital heart disease (CHD) diagnosis and evaluate the relationship between genetic variants and prenatal phenotypes. METHODS: A total of 235 fetuses with CHD were classified into three groups: A: isolated simple CHD, B: isolated complex CHD, and C: non-isolated CHD. All patients underwent karyotyping and copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq), with whole-exome sequencing (WES) performed when indicated. Statistical analyses conducted using IBM SPSS assessed the diagnostic performance of the genetic testing and detection rates across CHD subtypes. RESULTS: Karyotyping and CNV-seq revealed that chromosomal abnormality detection, particularly numerical abnormalities, was significantly associated with extracardiac anomalies (p < 0.05). In contrast, the detection rates of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) CNVs (CNV-seq, p = 0.384) and pathogenic gene variants (WES, p = 0.624) did not differ significantly among the three groups. The severity of intracardiac abnormalities, the presence of extracardiac anomalies, and the detection of genetic abnormalities significantly influenced parental decisions regarding pregnancy termination (p < 0.05). The combination of karyotyping and CNV-seq increased the detection rate by 5.11%. In karyotyping/CNV-seq-negative fetuses who underwent WES, WES increased the detection rate by 37.21% (16/43). CONCLUSION: Combined genetic testing significantly improved the detection rate and the detection of chromosomal numerical abnormalities was strongly associated with the presence of extracardiac anomalies. Parental decisions regarding pregnancy continuation were significantly influenced by the severity of intracardiac abnormalities, the presence of extracardiac anomalies, and the identification of genetic abnormalities.

papers.abstract_full: The etiological complexity of congenital heart disease (CHD) arises from the interaction between genetic and environmental factors. We hypothesized that environmental exposure could potentiate a genetic susceptibility, leading to an increased incidence of specific cardiac defects. To test this hypothesis, we used betaV59M+ female mice exhibiting severe hyperglycemia (>28 mmol/L) without dyslipidemia, a model we characterized that faithfully recapitulates human diabetic embryopathy. These females were crossed with males haploinsufficient for Nkx2-5, a transcription factor essential for cardiac development and implicated in human CHD. Our results show that the combination of genetic susceptibility and a hyperglycemic maternal environment (GxE) leads to a higher frequency and severity of cardiac malformations, including ventricular septal defects specifically involving the muscular septum, univentricular morphologies, and dilation with thinning of the myocardium. These structural abnormalities were associated with transcriptional changes affecting the contractile identity of the chamber myocardium. Single-nucleus multiomic profiling (snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq) of the E9.5 cardiac region revealed that the interaction between maternal diabetes and Nkx2-5 haploinsufficiency profoundly reshapes transcriptional and chromatin accessibility landscapes. These changes affect not only metabolic pathways, but also cell cycle progression in second heart field (SHF) progenitors, likely contributing to the observed structural cardiac defects. Multiomic integration further identifies a disrupted indirect Nkx2-5-Aldh1a2 regulatory axis in posterior SHF progenitors, while demonstrating that maternal diabetes selectively affects a restricted subset of Nkx2-5-dependent regulatory elements associated with cardiomyocyte maturation. Our findings establish a comprehensive single-cell multiomic resource that will facilitate the integration of human GWAS and other genomic datasets, enabling the identification and functional interpretation of disease-associated loci.

papers.abstract_full: Background:  Genetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions. Methods: Retrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals. Results: The cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]). Conclusions: Routine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Adult onset propionic acidemia (PA) is exceedingly rare, particularly when manifesting as dilated cardiomyopathy. CASE SUMMARY: A previously healthy 24-year-old man presented with cardiac dilatation and acute progressive heart failure. His condition was refractory to guideline-directed medical therapy, deteriorating to cardiogenic shock within 6 weeks. Plasma acylcarnitine profile revealed elevated propionylcarnitine and an increased propionylcarnitine-to-acetylcarnitine ratio. Urinary organic acid analysis showed elevated methylcitric acid. Whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous mutation in the PCCA gene. A diagnosis of PA presenting as metabolic cardiomyopathy was established. Cardiac function and hemodynamics improved with targeted metabolic treatment combined with guideline-directed medical therapy. DISCUSSION: Adult onset, metabolic cardiomyopathy because of PA is prone to being overlooked or misdiagnosed as refractory idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, potentially leading to premature escalation to advanced heart failure therapies. Early etiologic recognition and targeted metabolic treatment are crucial in the management of such cases. TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: Metabolic and genetic screening is recommended for patients with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, particularly in younger individuals. Early diagnosis and targeted intervention may preclude or delay the progression to left ventricular assist device implantation or heart transplantation in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy secondary to PA.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Although sodium voltage-gated channel alpha subunit 5 (SCN5A) was traditionally linked to electrophysiological disorders, growing evidence underscores its significant involvement in structural abnormalities. CASE SUMMARY: A young dilated cardiomyopathy patient presented with a distinctive electro-structural dual phenotype, characterized by progressive left ventricular systolic dysfunction, conduction disorders, and concomitant severe ventricular arrhythmias. Comorbidities included coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea. Genetic testing identified a de novo heterozygous nonsense variant in the SCN5A gene. Comprehensive management included guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure, antiarrhythmic agents, along with comorbidities management and risk factor modification. CONCLUSIONS: This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of dilated cardiomyopathy in young patients with multiple overlapping etiologies-genetic, ischemic, metabolic. A de novo SCN5A variant may contribute to the arrhythmic phenotype and progressive cardiomyopathy. TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: Beyond its classical electrophysiological role, SCN5A is increasingly implicated in structural remodeling. This case emphasizes the complexity of genotype-phenotype correlation and gene-environment interaction.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) presents with variable risk of life-threatening arrhythmias. Genetic diagnosis guides sudden death prevention strategies, but risk magnitude for arrhythmogenic genes remains unknown. This study leveraged the international Sarcomeric Human Cardiomyopathy Registry (SHaRe) to address this gap and improve risk stratification. METHODS: Effects of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in genes associated with DCM and ventricular arrhythmia on clinical events were analysed in DCM-SHaRe patients. Patients were stratified by presence of a P/LP variant in a high-arrhythmogenic risk gene (LMNA, DSP, FLNC, RBM20, PLN, SCN5A, DES, TMEM43), a low-arrhythmogenic risk gene (TTN, TNNT2, MYH7, others), or gene-elusive. Outcomes included age-, sex-, and baseline left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF)-adjusted risk of major ventricular arrhythmia (MVA), atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), death, and their composite. RESULTS: Among 2660 genotyped adults with DCM (mean diagnosis age 47 ± 15 years, 39.8% female), 434 (16%) had P/LP variants in high-arrhythmogenic genes, 451 (17%) in low-arrhythmogenic genes, and 1775 (67%) were gene-elusive. Compared with gene-elusive patients, patients with high-arrhythmogenic P/LP variants showed increased MVA [hazard ratio (HR) 3.25, 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.63-4.01], AF (HR 2.42, 95% CI 1.96-2.98), HF (HR 2.46, 95% CI 1.89-3.19), and composite (HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.69-2.29) risk, which remained significant after adjusting for age, sex, and LVEF. Patients with high-arrhythmogenic P/LP variants and LVEF ≥ 50% maintained increased MVA (HR 2.36, 95% CI 1.59-3.51) and composite (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.25-2.12) risk. CONCLUSIONS: Genetic testing enables powerful risk stratification for arrhythmias and HF in DCM independent of age, sex, or LVEF.

papers.abstract_full: Harel-Yoon syndrome is a rare mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic variants in ATAD3A, typically characterized by neonatal respiratory insufficiency, cataracts, developmental delay, hypotonia, and cerebellar atrophy. We report a pediatric patient with compound heterozygous missense variants in ATAD3A (c.655C>T, p.R219C and c.980G>C, p.R327P) who presented with an atypical phenotype manifested as early-onset congenital cataracts and progressive dilated cardiomyopathy. Notably the patient did not show typical neurological manifestations nor the cardiac presentations of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The maternally inherited c.655C>T variant was absent from population databases, while paternally inherited c.980G>C was previously associated with Harel-Yoon syndrome. In silico protein structure modeling demonstrated that the mutant ATAD3A hexamer showed a looser and more disorganized conformation compared to that of the wild-type, suggesting functional impairment. This case expands the phenotypic spectrum of ATAD3A-related disorders and highlights the importance of long-term surveillance in patients with ATAD3A variants, even in the absence of classical neurological features. In addition, our findings support the inclusion of ATAD3A in the genetic differential diagnosis for patients with congenital cataracts and cardiomyopathy.

papers.abstract_full: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the leading cause of birth defects; most critical (c)CHD newborns will develop neurodevelopmental disorders. Abnormal placental development may be involved, as genetics explains only 30% of sporadic CHD cases. Growing evidence suggests that placental dysfunction may result in heart and brain defects, as it shares a common early development. We hypothesized that newborns with critical CHD exhibit sex-specific alterations in placental mitochondrial biogenesis and function which may affect the fetal growth trajectory. Term placenta and paired umbilical cord (UC) blood were collected at birth from cCHD (n=16) and matched control (n=20) neonates. Mitochondrial lipid complex (phosphatidic acid (PA), phosphatidylglycerol (PG), cardiolipin (CL)), acylcarnitine metabolites and organic acids were determined in placenta by LC-MS/MS. Gene expressions of enzymes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics and lipid pathway were measured in placenta by RT-qPCR. Placental protein expressions of β-oxidation and OXPHOS were determined by Western Blot. Mitochondrial dynamics were reduced in cCHD placentas, particularly in male infants. Long-chain acylcarnitine (LC-acar) metabolites decreased in female cCHD placentas and increased in males, while they increased in both sexes in UC plasma. Malonate levels increased in cCHD placentas, affecting the TCA cycle. CL de novo synthesis was dysregulated in the cCHD placentas, though CL concentrations were similar in both groups. The cCHD placenta may compensate for cardiac defect in a potential sex-dependent manner, leading to an accumulation of LC-acylcarnitine in the UC plasma. Placental mitochondrial adaptation to metabolic needs may have a cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects.

Placental mitochondrial adaptation to metabolic needs may have a cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects.

papers.abstract_full: Background/Objectives: Noonan syndrome (NS) is characterized by marked phenotypic variability. Although the classical phenotype includes short stature, craniofacial dysmorphism, skeletal abnormalities, and congenital heart defects, some patients present with subtle or atypical manifestations, making clinical recognition challenging. Methods: This retrospective case series included six pediatric patients with molecularly confirmed NS managed at the Department of Endocrinology and Metabolic Diseases, Polish Mother's Memorial Hospital-Research Institute, Lodz, Poland. Medical records were reviewed for auxological data, phenotypic features, endocrine and skeletal assessment, cardiovascular findings, associated conditions, and multidisciplinary management. The aim of this study was to characterize the phenotypic diversity of NS in pediatric endocrine practice, with particular emphasis on growth patterns, endocrine and skeletal manifestations, and atypical clinical presentations. Results: The six patients demonstrated markedly heterogeneous clinical presentations. One boy exhibited the classical phenotype with severe short stature and pulmonary valve stenosis, whereas a girl with typical NS features maintained relatively preserved growth around the 3rd percentile. Another patient presented with progressive resorption of permanent incisor roots and a coexisting pathogenic NBN variant. A boy with LZTR1-associated NS and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) demonstrated a blended phenotype and height between the 25th and 50th percentiles. Two girls lacked characteristic NS dysmorphism and presented predominantly with growth impairment, accompanied by markedly low bone mass in one case and a prolonged diagnostic pathway in the other. GH deficiency was not identified in the evaluated patients, and rhGH therapy was initiated in three patients. Conclusions: NS encompasses a broad clinical spectrum, ranging from classical phenotypes to atypical presentations dominated by growth, skeletal, or dental abnormalities. Neither the absence of characteristic dysmorphism nor relatively preserved growth excludes the diagnosis, while coexisting genetic conditions may further modify the phenotype. Awareness of this heterogeneity is essential for appropriate recognition and individualized multidisciplinary care. In selected children with otherwise unexplained growth or atypical clinical findings, consideration of NS and genetic evaluation may help establish a unifying diagnosis and potentially shorten the diagnostic pathway.

papers.abstract_full: Developmental Systems Cardiology (DSC) conceptualizes congenital heart disease as a lifelong adaptive process shaped by interactions among biological, developmental, psychosocial, environmental, and healthcare systems. As survival has improved, contemporary challenges increasingly include neurodevelopment, psychosocial wellbeing, educational participation, healthcare engagement, and long-term adaptation, requiring multidimensional assessment beyond traditional physiological outcomes. This third article in the DSC series proposes a measurement framework for operationalizing adaptation across the lifespan. Rather than introducing new measurement domains or replacing established assessment recommendations, DSC provides an integrative architecture for linking existing measures across genomics and epigenomics, prenatal exposures, developmental physiology, neurocardiac interactions, family and social determinants, environmental influences, digital phenotyping, and healthcare-system context. Longitudinal measurement serves as a cross-cutting principle for characterizing adaptive trajectories and identifying periods of vulnerability and opportunity. Within this framework, adaptation is a dynamic, measurable process emerging through interactions among individuals, families, healthcare systems, and broader environments. Measurement therefore encompasses developmental functioning, resilience, participation, quality of life, healthcare transitions, and implementation outcomes alongside biological and clinical indicators. Established domain-specific standards, including neurodevelopmental assessment recommendations, can populate this broader architecture. This approach emphasizes integration rather than instrument development, while preserving the specificity and utility of established measures within individual domains. Its proposed contribution lies in organizing multidimensional measurement to better understand how adaptive and maladaptive trajectories emerge and evolve across development.

papers.abstract_full: Duplications of distal 20q are uncommon and the connection to oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum (OAVS) is still not clear. In this paper we describe a family-based cytogenetic case of a geographically isolated community in Northern Italy. Clinical data, pedigree information, and cytogenetic report from the proband were collected. Relatives were examined for OAVS-related features. Subtelomeric FISH analysis was performed with probes for 20qter and D22S1726 using peripheral blood lymphocytes to assess the rearrangement in detail. Descriptive statistics with 95% confidence intervals were computed. FISH demonstrated additional terminal material on der (22) consistent with a complex subtelomeric rearrangement and partial trisomy of 20qter. Among the 30 evaluated relatives, 15 (50.0%; exact 95% CI, 31.3-68.7) carried the rearrangement. Of these, 5 (33.3%; exact 95% CI, 11.8-61.6) exhibited features within the oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, including preauricular tags, microtia or aural atresia, hemi-facial microsomia, ocular anomalies, vertebral defects, congenital heart disease, and hearing impairment. FISH does not provide information about the duplication segment or genes involved; therefore, MYT1 inclusion into the duplication cannot be confirmed and requires further chromosomal microarray, SNP-array, MLPA or genome sequencing analysis. In this pedigree, the findings support the distal 20qter/20q13.33 as a possible candidate genomic region associated with OAVS-related features and support high-resolution genomic studies and genetic counselling in affected families.

papers.abstract_full: Recent advances in high-resolution genomic technologies have revealed that several syndromes are associated with submicroscopic chromosomal deletions and, less frequently, duplications, thereby substantially contributing to the functional annotation of the human genome. Among these structural variants, recurrent microdeletions or microduplications often disrupt dosage-sensitive genes, leading to shared phenotypic outcomes in affected individuals. While features such as congenital heart defects, neurodevelopmental delays, and intellectual disability (ID) have been extensively studied, phenotypes resulting in olfactory dysfunction remain largely underexplored. Here, we review reported cases of copy number variants (CNVs) in patients with isolated or syndromic olfactory impairment and stratify the strength of associations between CNVs and olfactory dysfunction using predefined evidence levels. The available evidence ranges from well-supported loci with documented human olfactory phenotypes and mechanistic evidence to hypothesis-generating observations based primarily on isolated cases or biological plausibility. By distinguishing these levels of evidence, we highlight both established dosage-sensitive pathways involved in olfactory development and major limitations of the current literature, including incomplete olfactory phenotyping and the difficulty of interpreting large multigenic CNVs. This framework may facilitate more rigorous genotype-phenotype interpretation in congenital and syndromic olfactory disorders.

papers.abstract_full: INTRODUCTION: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is one of the most common congenital heart defects but its genetic basis remains incompletely defined. Extracellular matrix components play key roles in outflow tract (OFT) and valve development, but their contribution to BAV is not fully established. Following the analysis of a cohort of BAV patients, we identified a family harbouring a rare human ELASTIN (ELN) variant (p.Gln691X). Here, we investigated the pathogenicity of this variant using an in vivo zebrafish model. METHODS: We generated a zebrafish elna/b double knockout (KO) using an RNAless CRISPR Cas9 strategy to avoid genetic compensation. Cardiovascular morphology and function were assessed in mutant embryos. To evaluate pathogenicity of the human ELN p.Gln691X variant, mutant and control embryos were rescued by mRNA injection encoding either WT human ELN or the p.Gln691X variant. RESULTS: elna/b double KO zebrafish exhibited cardiovascular defects including OFT anomalies, reduced stroke volume and dysmorphic aortic valves, highlighting Elastin's critical role in cardiac development. We then used this model to test the ELN variant identified in the BAV family. We found that wild-type ELN mRNA was able to restore normal cardiac function and morphology, whereas the variant ELN mRNA failed to do so. DISCUSSION: Our study establishes a robust in vivo model to assess ELN variant pathogenicity and provides evidence linking ELASTIN to BAV, opening new avenues for uncovering the genetic mechanisms underlying BAV.

papers.abstract_full: The ryanodine receptor 1 (RYR1) gene encodes a protein channel located on the terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle, thereby playing a key role in regulation of skeletal muscle contraction. RYR1 gene mutations may result in inherited neuromuscular conditions with a wide range of clinical manifestations including profound hypotonia, proximal muscle weakness, facial weakness, respiratory involvement, and orthopedic disorders (scoliosis, hip dislocation, and arthrogryposis). Affected individuals may also be malignant hyperthermia susceptible. We present an infant with RYR1 gene mutation who presented for anesthetic care during cardiac surgery for congenital heart disease. The clinical spectrum of RYR1 gene mutation disorders is presented, previous reports of anesthetic care reviewed, and options for perioperative care discussed.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract      Background    :  Congenital heart defects (CHDs) are the most common birth anomalies worldwide, with a substantial but incompletely characterized genetic contribution. Coarctation of the aorta (CoA) is a common CHD for which the diagnostic yield of comprehensive genomic testing remains insufficiently defined.    Methods    :  In a single-center Swedish cohort, 19 pediatric patients with CoA with or without associated aortic arch hypoplasia, bicuspid aortic valve, or additional simple CHDs, and no prior genetic diagnosis were prospectively enrolled at the time of surgical repair and underwent whole-genome sequencing (WGS).    Results    :  WGS identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 3/19 patients (16%), and genetic variants of uncertain significance were identified in 3/19 patients (16%). Thus, genomic findings were reported in 6 patients (32%) overall, although only the pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were considered diagnostic. Several identified diagnoses had not been suspected based on clinical assessment alone, highlighting the limited sensitivity of phenotypic evaluation during early infancy.    Conclusions    : The proportion of genetically explained CoA in this surgically treated cohort supports the consideration of genetic testing, particularly in individuals with CoA accompanied by other congenital cardiac defects or extracardiac manifestations. Importantly, an underlying genetic disorder may be present despite the absence of overt clinical signs during infancy. Recognition of this possibility should encourage thorough phenotypic assessment and expanded clinical evaluation to identify potential genetic syndromes. Early genetic diagnosis may improve clinical management, surveillance, and genetic counseling for affected families.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: FHL2 is critical for cardiac development, and its variants are associated with early-onset severe dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), though such reports remain rare. CASE PRESENTATION: The patient was a 30-day-old male infant admitted with a 3-day history of cough, a 2-day history of poor feeding, and lethargy lasting half a day. Echocardiography revealed left ventricular enlargement, with a minimum left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of only 13%, and endocardial thickening. Genetic testing identified a heterozygous missense variant c.391C>T (p.Arg131Cys) in FHL2. This variant was confirmed to be de novo. According to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines, it was classified as likely pathogenic, suggestive of DCM. After heart failure management and other symptomatic treatments, the patient's clinical symptoms improved. However, LVEF remained low at 15.5% during the 6-month follow-up. CONCLUSION: The heterozygous missense variant c.391C>T (p.Arg131Cys) in FHL2 is associated with DCM in this patient, and the endocardial thickening may represent a secondary change. However, we acknowledge that without pathological examination of the explanted heart or endomyocardial biopsy, the possibility of primary endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE) cannot be completely excluded. This study emphasizes the clinical importance of distinguishing true primary EFE from secondary EFE-like endocardial changes associated with severe DCM, and genetic testing is valuable for their differential diagnosis.

papers.abstract_full: Inherited arrhythmias and cardiomyopathies are leading causes of sudden cardiac death in young individuals. Although global registries and genetic databases have advanced diagnosis and prevention globally, data from the Middle East (ME) remain limited and fragmented. This review synthesizes clinical and genetic evidence on long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and dilated cardiomyopathy across the ME. A defining feature of ME cohorts is the high prevalence of consanguinity, which shapes a distinctive genetic and clinical landscape across these conditions. Autosomal recessive inheritance is consistently enriched, producing homozygous genotypes, which frequently manifest as earlier onset and more aggressive clinical phenotypes compared with those in non-ME populations. Population-specific founder variants have been identified across multiple conditions, whereas consanguineous pedigrees have contributed to the discovery of novel disease genes and recessive mechanisms that expand the global genetic landscape of inherited cardiovascular disease. However, a disproportionately high burden of variants of uncertain significance persists across conditions, driven largely by underrepresentation of ME populations in global genomic reference databases. Emerging large-scale genome initiatives such as the Qatar Biobank, the Egyptian Genome Project, and the Greater Middle East Variome offer a viable path toward ancestry-specific variant interpretation. Strengthening regional registries, genomic resources, and family-based screening programs will be essential to improving risk stratification and prevention of sudden cardiac death in the ME.

papers.abstract_full: Inherited cardiovascular diseases (ICVDs) are a broad category of hereditary disorders resulting from pathogenic mutations that alter cardiac anatomy, electrical conduction, and metabolic pathways. The main types include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), cardiac channelopathies, and familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) and are associated with heart failure, malignant arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death, particularly in young people. Current treatments, such as pharmacological therapies, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, and heart transplantation, have significantly improved outcomes; however, these treatments are mainly targeted toward symptom control and the prevention of complications without correcting the underlying genetic defects. Recent advancements in genome editing have transformed precision cardiovascular care, with clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based technologies emerging as potential methods for targeting and modifying disease-causing variants. Emerging platforms, such as base editing, prime editing, and epigenome editing, have widened the therapeutic potential of genome engineering by enhancing editing precision and reducing some of the constraints of the traditional CRISPR-Cas9 strategy. In the setting of inherited cardiovascular disorders, promising early results have been obtained in preclinical studies using human induced pluripotent stem cell and animal models, including correction of MYBPC3 and MYH7 mutations in HCM; targeting of TTN-, RBM20-, and LMNA-associated mechanisms in DCM; restoration of ion channel function in inherited arrhythmia syndromes; and modulation of lipid-related genes such as PCSK9, LDLR, and ANGPTL3 in FH. However, major challenges remain, including off-target effects, effective delivery to cardiac tissues, immunological responses, interpretation of genetic variants, and ethical concerns. This review provides a translational, integrated view of the evolution of CRISPR-based genome editing technologies, their application to ICVDs, current preclinical and clinical advances, and the challenges that need to be addressed to achieve safe and effective translation into cardiovascular therapeutics.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Most atrial septal defects (ASDs) occur sporadically, but familial cases can occur and carry a 10% risk of transmission to offspring. CASE SUMMARY: We describe a 3-generation family with autosomal dominant secundum ASD and conduction system disease related to a novel NKX2-5 variant (c.300del; p.Asp101Thrfs∗75). The index patient, a 58-year-old woman with prior ASD repair and mitral valve replacement, presented with chronotropic incompetence, atrial fibrillation, left bundle branch block, and prolonged pauses, leading to pacemaker implantation. Her mother had an ASD, atrial fibrillation, left bundle branch block, and pulmonary arterial hypertension. The proband's daughter also had an ASD. Genetic testing revealed a novel NKX2-5 pathogenic variant in all 3 patients. REVIEW SUMMARY: The combination of an ASD and conduction system disease represents the most common phenotype in patients with pathogenic NKX2-5 variants. TAKE-HOME MESSAGE: A thorough family history and genetic testing are needed when evaluating patients with ASD and concurrent conduction system abnormalities.

Cardiovascular damage in MS has serious complications such as aneurysms and aortic dissection (AD), which increase during pregnancy. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the cardiovascular and clinical status of women with Marfan syndrome and pregnancy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Retrospective study in women with MS or other connective tissue diseases (CTD) classified according to the 2010 Ghent criteria. RESULTS: One hundred women were included, 35 were admitted as pediatric patients, and 65 as adults. Ten women without medical records were excluded. Forty-eight non-pregnant women and 46 pregnant women were analyzed. 20 births, 26 cesarean sections, 9 preeclampsia, and 14 miscarriages. Of the total group, 14 had con-genital heart disease, 36 had AD, 47 had aortic regurgitation, 22 had mitral valve regurgitation, 15 had tricuspid valve regurgitation, 39 had valve prolapse, 67 had surgeries, and 15 had stents. 19 died, 5 due to aneurysm rupture, 4 had AD, 3 had cardiogenic shock, 5 had septic shock, and 2 had hypovolemic shock. CONCLUSIONS: Cardiovascular damage in pregnancies of women with MS or CTD is complex. The diagnosis of MS is late in some cases; it is at the time of delivery, and genetic counseling is not timely. papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic disorder associated with recurrent infections and irreversible airway damage. No single diagnostic test exists, necessitating use of a diagnostic algorithm that varies internationally. This retrospective study aimed to describe the clinical characteristics of patients, and algorithm used to diagnose PCD in New South Wales between 2014 and 2024. METHODS: A retrospective review of patients diagnosed with PCD at Concord Repatriation General Hospital (CRGH) from 2014 to 2024 was performed. RESULTS: This study included 52 patients with median age of diagnosis 7.0 years. The diagnostic algorithm consists of nasal nitric oxide (nNO) in patients > 5 years, and nasal brushings for high-speed video microscopy (HSVMA), immunofluorescence (IF) and electron microscopy (EM). Whole exome sequencing is not routine and was performed in 33% of the cohort. The diagnosis was confirmed by a multidisciplinary team that considered the test results and clinical phenotype. Non-diagnostic results occurred in 14% (nNO), 15% (HSVMA), 41% (IF) and 30% (EM) of patients eventually diagnosed with PCD or PCD "highly likely". Cumulatively, 56% of patients had at least one non-diagnostic result. Of the 17 patients who underwent whole exome sequencing with a PCD panel, 41% had diagnostic genetic results. CONCLUSION: Ciliary studies continue to be the mainstay of PCD diagnosis at CRGH. Although genetic testing is not part of the CRGH diagnostic algorithm, the CRGH algorithm has similar diagnostic performance to the ERS and ATS guidelines.

papers.abstract_full: Arsenic (As) is a widespread environmental contaminant, with exposure occurring primarily through contaminated food and water or cigarette smoke. Maternal exposure to As represents a significant risk factor for congenital heart disease in offspring. However, the mechanisms underlying As-induced developmental cardiotoxicity remain poorly defined. Pluripotent stem cells provide an excellent platform for studying mechanisms of developmental toxicity. Embryoid bodies (EBs) derived from stem cells, can recapitulate many key events of early embryogenesis including germ layers specification. Human cardiomyocytes are derived from mesodermal progenitors. NKX2- 5 governs cardiac specification and morphogenesis, and its mutation produces atrial and ventricular defects in humans. Using an NKX2-5 reporter stem cell line, we modeled mesoderm differentiation in EBs and cardiac induction in a 2D cardiomyocyte differentiation system. In an 8-day differentiation protocol, As (0.05 μM; 3.75 ppb) significantly suppressed cardiomyocyte differentiation and cardiac induction. However, As increased mesodermal markers (HAND1, SNAI2, HOPX) gene expression. In contrast, cardiac-specific genes, including NKX2-5, GATA4, Troponin T, and α-Actinin, were markedly downregulated in the presence of As. As also reduced expression of genes related to cardiac induction, fibroblast function, and vascular markers in the cardiac organoid model. As impaired cardiomyocyte maturation related gene expressions at concentrations without affecting cardiomyocyte proliferation. In a zebrafish model of early heart development, As increased heart rate and disrupted ion channel gene expression. In conclusion, As inhibits ESC differentiation into cardiomyocytes and disrupts cardiomyocyte maturation. Combining stem cell–derived models with zebrafish exposure, this study illuminates adverse outcome pathways for As-induced congenital heart defect.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Radiation-induced heart disease (RIHD) may develop months to years following radiation therapy for cancers near the heart such as lung or breast cancer. Several mouse models of RIHD exist to study the pathogenesis of disease, but to our knowledge no studies have examined whether sex differences exist in RIHD in mice. METHODS: Female and male BALB/cJ mice received a single whole-heart dose of 22 Gy (Gy) radiation via a C5 collimator vs. sham controls that received 0 Gy, anesthesia and were placed in the X-ray machine for the same length of time. Endpoints were examined at 24 h (innate), day 10 (acute) and day 35 (chronic) post irradiation. RESULTS: Females and males developed dsDNA breaks from radiation at day 10 but females had more damage than males (p < 0.001). Vessel area and wall thickness were increased by radiation at day 10 and 35 but vessel area was greater in irradiated males than females at day 35 (p = 0.003). Bulk RNA sequencing of the heart at day 10 revealed that females and males developed similar gene pathway responses to radiation by upregulating cellular repair pathways and developing mitochondrial dysfunction. However, females upregulated the master regulator of mitochondrial function, Pgc1α (p = 0.0001), suggesting possible improved mitochondrial repair in females. By day 35, females developed mild cardiomyopathy while males developed myocardial and perivascular fibrosis and inflammatory dilated cardiomyopathy (iDCM). CONCLUSIONS: We observed sex differences in most cardiac parameters that we examined following radiation exposure. BALB/c males exposed to 22 Gy radiation developed iDCM by day 35 while females developed mild cardiomyopathy. Further research is needed to better understand mechanisms driving sex differences in RIHD using translational animal models. Radiation therapy used to treat cancers near the heart, such as breast and lung cancer, can sometimes cause heart damage months or years later, a condition known as radiation-induced heart disease (RIHD). Although mouse models are commonly used to study RIHD, little is known about whether males and females respond differently to radiation exposure. In this study, male and female BALB/cJ mice received a single radiation dose directed at the heart and were compared with non-irradiated control mice. Researchers examined early and later effects of radiation over a 35-day period. Both sexes experienced radiation-induced DNA damage in heart cells, but females showed greater DNA damage than males. Radiation also increased blood vessel size and heart enlargement in both sexes, although these changes were more pronounced in males. Gene expression analysis showed that males and females activated many of the same repair pathways after radiation and both showed reduced mitochondrial function. However, females increased expression of Pgc1α, a key regulator of mitochondrial health, suggesting they may have a greater ability to repair mitochondrial damage. By 35 days after radiation exposure, males developed heart fibrosis and inflammatory dilated cardiomyopathy, while females developed mild heart disease without evidence of inflammation or fibrosis. These findings demonstrate important sex-specific differences in the cardiac response to radiation and highlight the need for further research to understand the biological mechanisms underlying these differences.

After myocardial infarction, cardiomyocytes are lost permanently because the surviving cells are terminally differentiated and post-mitotic. papers.abstract_full: The adult mammalian heart does not regenerate. After myocardial infarction, cardiomyocytes are lost permanently because the surviving cells are terminally differentiated and post-mitotic. Regenerative vertebrates such as zebrafish and newts retain proliferative, centriole-bearing cardiomyocytes and repair the heart completely, whereas mammals lose this capacity within the first postnatal week. I propose that the centriole functions as a differentiation ratchet: a heritable structural input that couples proliferative potential to centriole integrity through the mitotic surveillance pathway (MSP). The strongest natural evidence comes from the heart. Shortly after birth, mammalian cardiomyocytes undergo programmed centrosome disassembly, with pericentriolar material relocating to the nuclear envelope. Pharmacological depletion of centrioles is sufficient to drive the post-mitotic transition in human cardiomyocytes, and failure of this step is pathogenic: a mutation in the centrosomal gene RTTN causes infantile dilated cardiomyopathy. Because the adult cardiomyocyte is one of the few naturally and permanently acentriolar somatic cells, it offers a ready-made testbed for asking whether the ratchet can be reversed. A single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis of the developing human heart (fetal, young and adult) presented here shows that this shutdown is actively installed during maturation rather than a passive decay: adult cardiomyocytes reduce their centriolar program—PLK4, CEP192, SASS6, STIL and NEK2 are all down-regulated—while the p53 effector p21 (CDKN1A) is elevated, the signature of a p53-maintained post-mitotic lock. The roadmap proceeds in three steps, all conducted in cell culture: (i) release the G0 lock and assess TRIM37 and PLK1 status; (ii) restore a licensed centriole from an autologous low-entropy adult stem cell, with PLK1 and Ect2 co-delivery; and (iii) enforce a strict safety gate that includes TRIM37, p53 pathway, and contractile function assessment. Eight pre-registered, falsifiable hypotheses are stated below, and the principal risks are analyzed.

papers.title: From inherited susceptibility to tumor state: toward a stage-aware architecture for genomic risk stratification in prostate cancer.
papers.abstract: Prostate cancer risk is currently represented by two largely separate genomic layers. Germline polygenic scores estimate inherited susceptibility before diagnosis, whereas tumor genomic and transcriptomic classifiers estimate biological aggressiveness and treatment response after tissue acquisition. Artificial intelligence can connect these layers, but simply concatenating high-dimensional features is unlikely to produce transportable clinical tools. papers.abstract_full: Prostate cancer risk is currently represented by two largely separate genomic layers. Germline polygenic scores estimate inherited susceptibility before diagnosis, whereas tumor genomic and transcriptomic classifiers estimate biological aggressiveness and treatment response after tissue acquisition. Artificial intelligence can connect these layers, but simply concatenating high-dimensional features is unlikely to produce transportable clinical tools. This Mini Review examines how biologically informed machine learning, single-cell and spatial atlases, whole-omics response models, and validated tissue classifiers are reshaping prostate cancer risk stratification. We argue that the most useful architecture is a stage-aware system: ancestry-calibrated germline risk first modifies screening intensity; tissue or liquid-biopsy models then resolve tumor state; and longitudinal molecular measurements update risk under treatment. Evidence is strongest for polygenic enrichment of screening populations and for locked transcriptomic classifiers tested in randomized-trial cohorts. By contrast, many multi-omics models remain retrospective, dataset-dependent, and weakly calibrated across ancestry, disease stage, and specimen type. Progress requires explicit clinical decision points, external and prospective validation, uncertainty reporting, ancestry-aware calibration, and comparisons against simpler clinicopathological models. A unified framework should therefore treat artificial intelligence not as a single prognostic score, but as an auditable sequence of genomic updates that links inherited susceptibility to evolving tumor biology.

papers.abstract: Hypertension represents a major modifiable cardiovascular risk factor with increasing global prevalence. While numerous prognostic models for incident hypertension have been developed, their clinical implementation remains limited, suggesting a gap between model development and practical application. This study aimed to synthesize evidence from systematic reviews on multivariable prognostic models estimating the future risk of incident hypertension among initially normotensive individuals, evalu…
papers.abstract_full: Hypertension represents a major modifiable cardiovascular risk factor with increasing global prevalence. While numerous prognostic models for incident hypertension have been developed, their clinical implementation remains limited, suggesting a gap between model development and practical application. This study aimed to synthesize evidence from systematic reviews on multivariable prognostic models estimating the future risk of incident hypertension among initially normotensive individuals, evaluating methodological quality, predictive performance, validation status, calibration reporting, and clinical utility. We conducted an umbrella review, searching six databases from January 2000 to March 2026. Systematic reviews (SRs) evaluating multivariable prognostic models for incident hypertension with documented external validation evidence were included; reviews mixing prognostic and cross-sectional diagnostic screening models were retained only when eligible prognostic evidence could be distinguished and were examined in sensitivity synthesis. Methodological quality was assessed using ROBIS, and primary-study risk of bias was extracted from PROBAST/CHARMS assessments reported by the included reviews. Six SRs (three with meta-analyses) identified 162 unique models reported as prognostic. Models were categorized as traditional statistical (60%), machine learning (30%), and genetic/polygenic risk score-based (10%). Reported pooled AUCs were 0.78 (95% CI 0.76-0.80) for traditional models and 0.82 (95% CI 0.77-0.86) for machine learning models, but all quantitative summaries showed extreme heterogeneity (I2 > 99%) and should therefore be interpreted descriptively rather than as stable estimates of clinical performance. Only 21 of 94 models with extractable validation information (22%) underwent at least one external validation, and only seven of 162 unique models were externally validated more than once. Calibration was reported in a minority of models, and no published clinical-impact studies evaluating the use of these models in routine practice were identified. The field should avoid prioritizing additional de novo model derivation in already well-represented settings and should redirect resources toward external validation, recalibration, clinical-impact evaluation, and implementation of the most robust existing models in primary care.

papers.abstract_full: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) are widely used to quantify genetic predisposition to complex traits, and their predictive accuracy can be enhanced by incorporating functional annotations into single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) effect-size estimation. Existing approaches typically assume linear relationships between annotations and SNP effects, neglecting predictive aleatoric variance and potential nonlinear regulatory interactions. To evaluate the gains of nonlinear and uncertainty-aware modeling, we developed DeepU-PRS, a deep ensemble framework that extends the linear BLD-LDAK model with a neural network trained on functional annotations to jointly estimate SNP heritability and its aleatoric uncertainty, which are then integrated into a Bayesian PRS model. Across 28 continuous and 8 disease phenotypes in the UK Biobank, DeepU-PRS improved the mean continuous R2 by approximately 10% over linear BLD-LDAK, with the largest gains for traits whose association signals were concentrated, whereas the more diffuse disease traits favored BLD-LDAK. These patterns were reproduced in individual-level data from All of Us. Against a panel of established methods (C + T, Lassosum, PRS-CS, LDpred-funct, and SBayesRC), DeepU-PRS was among the strongest single methods on continuous traits, and ensembles combining DeepU-PRS with the linear baseline and SBayesRC further improved accuracy, indicating complementary predictive signal. These findings highlight the value of modeling nonlinear and uncertain regulatory effects to advance PRS prediction.

papers.abstract_full: Allostatic load (AL), a composite measure of multisystem dysregulation associated with chronic stress, has been linked to lung cancer risk. However, its joint effects with genetic susceptibility and the biological pathways underlying this relationship remain unclear. We conducted a prospective cohort study of 336,945 UK Biobank participants to assess associations between AL and lung cancer incidence and its histological subtypes. A polygenic risk score was constructed to evaluate the joint associations of AL and genetic susceptibility. We further assessed whether AL provided incremental risk stratification beyond established low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening eligibility frameworks and integrated plasma proteomic data using machine learning, enrichment, and mediation analyses. We found that higher AL was associated with an increased risk of lung cancer (per-unit HR = 1.073, 95% CI: 1.053-1.094; Low vs. Normal HR = 1.284, 95% CI: 1.065-1.547; High vs. Normal HR = 1.629, 95% CI: 1.347-1.971). Subtype analyses revealed the strongest effect for small-cell lung cancer (SCLC), with significant associations also observed for lung adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. High AL combined with high genetic risk was associated with a 136.9% increased risk (HR = 2.369, 95% CI: 1.565-3.583), without evidence of interaction. AL provided additional risk discrimination beyond established LDCT screening eligibility criteria. Proteomic analyses identified 111 AL-associated proteins and 34 proteins with potential mediation signal, including HGF, RARRES2, and GDF15, implicating inflammatory, metabolic, and growth factor-related processes as biological correlates of the AL-lung cancer association. In conclusion, higher AL was independently associated with lung cancer risk, particularly SCLC. Integrative proteomic analyses provided exploratory evidence for biological pathways that may link cumulative physiological dysregulation to lung carcinogenesis. Incorporating AL, as a composite biomarker reflecting cumulative physiological burden, into risk models may improve risk stratification and help identify individuals at elevated risk.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Childhood-onset attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) persists in 28% to 58% of individuals, and is associated with adverse long-term outcomes, like additional psychiatric diagnoses and lower educational attainment. Knowing early life predictors for adverse long-term outcomes might help develop preventive measures, but too few have been identified using conventional statistical models. The current study investigated the potential of machine learning in identifying predictors for ADHD persistence and long-term functioning of adults with childhood-onset ADHD. METHOD: A total of 133 adults (Mage = 29.53, SDage = 2.83, 75% males) from an 18-year prospective cohort study were assessed on ADHD persistence and long-term functioning. Machine learning models were developed using cross-validation, with and without additional resampling, and compared to a conventional logistic/linear regression model. With SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) we explored model behavior. Childhood predictors encompassed ADHD symptoms and treatment, other psychopathology, cognition, somatic characteristics, ADHD polygenic risk score, and parental demographics and psychopathology. RESULTS: Performance of all models for ADHD persistence and functioning (quality of life) was low. Best performing models included the logistic regression model with resampling for ADHD persistence (AUC'sall models = .52-.58; AUClogistic regression, resampling = .58), and the ridge regression model for long-term functioning (R2'sall models = -0.36-0.02; R2'sridge regression = .02, RMSE's all models = 2.07-2.42; RMSE'sridge regression = 2.07). CONCLUSIONS: Findings highlight the complexity of predicting long-term outcomes of ADHD. papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: The precise cause of ulcerative colitis (UC) is still unclear. While transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channels are increasingly linked to UC pathophysiology, the comprehensive roles of TRP channel-related genes are not well understood. This study aimed to systematically identify TRP channel-related biomarkers and develop novel diagnostic and therapeutic targets for UC. METHODS: Transcriptomic data were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Machine learning algorithms were applied to select signature genes from the overlap between differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and a curated set of 111 transient receptor potential (TRP) channel-related genes. A diagnostic nomogram incorporating signature genes was constructed, and its performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA). The cellular landscape was characterized using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) combined with pseudotime trajectory inference and cell-cell communication analysis. Key results were further validated in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced murine colitis model by flow cytometry, multiplex immunohistochemistry, western blotting, and quantitative real-time PCR. RESULTS: Five TRP channel-related feature genes (IL-1β, PIK3R3, ADCY3, ADCY7, and TRPV1) were identified. In UC, IL-1β, PIK3R3, ADCY3, and ADCY7 were notably upregulated, while TRPV1 was markedly downregulated. The nomogram, utilizing these five feature genes, exhibited outstanding discriminatory capability (AUC = 0.993) and provided enhanced net clinical benefit. scRNA-seq analysis identified B and plasma cells as the most significantly expanded pathogenic population, exhibiting acquired bidirectional crosstalk with epithelial cells in UC. Pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed that IL-1β and PIK3R3 were mainly concentrated during the initial developmental phases of B and plasma cells. In the DSS-induced colitis model, there was a notable increase in B-cell infiltration, accompanied by significant upregulation of IL-1β and Pik3r3 at both protein and mRNA levels, with confirmed colocalization with Cd19+ B cells. CONCLUSION: This study identified five TRP channel-related biomarkers and created a high-performance diagnostic nomogram for UC. The study underscores the pivotal role of B and plasma cells, identifying IL-1β and PIK3R3 as early-activated genes in pathogenic B-cell responses, thus offering new diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets for UC.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: This study aimed to analyze the expression characteristics of CD40L on peripheral blood T lymphocytes in patients with sepsis and explore its value in assessing disease severity and prognosis. METHODS: This prospective study collected blood samples and clinical data from adult sepsis patients admitted to the Department of Critical Care Medicine at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University between March 2023 and March 2024, with the primary endpoint being 28-day mortality. Multivariate Cox regression analysis was performed to evaluate the association between T lymphocyte CD40L expression and 28-day mortality. Additionally, machine learning algorithms were applied to determine the importance of CD40L-related features, and latent class mixed model analysis was conducted to identify different expression trajectories. RESULTS: A total of 112 sepsis patients were included, with a 28-day mortality rate of 20.5%. CD40L expression levels on peripheral blood CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes were significantly higher in sepsis patients compared to healthy controls. Three distinct expression patterns were identified for both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Patients with persistently low CD40L expression levels had significantly lower survival rates (P < 0.001). Moreover, multivariate Cox analysis identified day 1 CD40L levels on CD4+ (HR 0.712, 95% CI 0.606-0.837, P < 0.001) and CD8+ T cells (HR 0.593, 95% CI 0.481-0.731, P < 0.001) as an independent predictor of 28-day mortality. ROC analysis revealed strong associations between day 1 CD40L expression and mortality, with AUCs of 0.847 and 0.875, respectively. Finally, the combination of CD40L expression with SOFA scores improved clinical decision-making compared to SOFA scoring alone. CONCLUSION: Peripheral blood T lymphocyte CD40L was identified as an independent predictor of 28-day mortality in sepsis patients. Identifying distinct expression trajectories of CD40L in peripheral blood T lymphocytes can effectively assist in predicting short-term prognosis in patients with sepsis.

papers.abstract_full: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) represents over 90% of diabetes cases globally, posing a growing public health crisis with an estimated 783 million adults projected to be affected by 2045. This condition arises from a complex interplay of insulin resistance, progressive pancreatic β-cell dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation, strongly influenced by genetic predisposition, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and poor dietary habits. While genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified key susceptibility loci, including TCF7L2, PPARG, and KCNJ11, these varian0ts explain only ~10% of T2D heritability, underscoring the critical role of gene-environment interactions. This review synthesizes current evidence on the genetic, nutrigenomic, and epigenetic mechanisms underlying T2D pathogenesis and progression. We examine how dietary components, such as flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, and bioactive compounds from natural products, modulate gene expression via transcription factors and influence insulin sensitivity, oxidative stress, and inflammation. Furthermore, we explore the emerging role of epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation, histone acetylation, and chromatin remodeling, in mediating the lasting effects of hyperglycemia and environmental factors on T2D risk. The potential of epigenetic biomarkers for early diagnosis, patient stratification, and personalized therapy is discussed. Finally, we highlight how next-generation sequencing and artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and deep learning models, are advancing multi-omics data integration, enabling improved T2D subtype classification, prognosis prediction, and the development of precision nutrition and pharmacoepigenetic strategies.

papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: To develop a diagnostic model for primary Sjögren syndrome (pSS) utilizing transcriptomics-based machine learning techniques, and to explore potential therapeutic targets. METHODS: We selected patients diagnosed with pSS and control subjects with salivary gland samples from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database for transcriptome sequencing. This was complemented by methylation sequencing data, followed by weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) in conjunction with clinical data to identify candidate diagnostic genes. Subsequently, we refined the gene list using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), random forest (RF), Gaussian mixed model (GMM), and support vector machine (SVM). Ultimately, we constructed a composite diagnostic model for pSS employing SVM, neural networks (NN), Logistic regression (LR), decision trees (DT), adaptive boosting (AdaBoost), bootstrap aggregating (Bagging), random forest, and Naive Bayes classifiers, totaling eight distinct machine learning algorithms, and predicted drug targets. RESULTS: Through differential gene screening combined with WGCNA analysis of the GEO database, we identified 12 key genes. Further variable selection via machine learning techniques yielded four significant genes: VNN2, NAPSB, SAMSN1, and MS4A1. The area under curve (AUC) values were calculated for each gene: AUCVNN2 =0.865, AUCNAPSB=0.896, AUCSAMSN1 =0.872, AUCMS4A1 =0.914, all demonstrating diagnostic relevance. We then employed these machine learning methods to construct a composite diagnostic model, and F1 score (the harmonic mean of precision and recall rate) was used to evaluate the prediction performance of each model in the internal test set. The top-performing models included those based on SVM polynomial kernel models, SVM linear kernel models, random forest approaches, and Naive Bayes classification as determined through ranking criteria based on AUC comparisons; notably, both SVM polynomial kernel models and linear kernel models exhibited superior AUC values compared with individual genes alone. The external validation set, SVM polynomial kernel function model in GSE159574, AUC=0.865 (95%CI: 0.728-1.000), sensitivity 0.812, specificity 0.846; The AUC of SVM polynomial kernel model in GSE173808, AUC=0.896 (95%CI: 0.797-0.996), the sensitivity was 0.778, and the specificity was 1.000. In order to facilitate clinical diagnosis, we verified that the AUC of the SVM polynomial kernel function model in the peripheral blood GSE84844 dataset was 0.827 (95%CI: 0.719-0.934), the sensitivity was 0.867, and the specificity was 0.767. Thus, our proposed model demonstrated robust diagnostic capability for pSS. Additionally, our investigation into potential drug targets indicated that these four identified genes served as targets for glucocorticoid therapies while curcumin emerged as a promising candidate agent in treating pSS. CONCLUSION: This research identifies VNN2, NAPSB, SAMSN1, and MS4A1 as specific biomarkers for diagnosing pSS, thereby enriching existing genetic markers relevant to diagnosis while establishing a reliable composite diagnostic framework which underscores the close association between methylation processes in the pathogenesis of pSS, offering novel insights into early diagnosis strategies along with prospective treatment avenues.

papers.abstract_full: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have linked thousands of loci to common diseases, yet for non-coding variants, which constitute the vast majority of the signal, the cell types and states through which individual risk variants act remain largely unknown. Here, we develop GEMS (GWAS Effect Mechanisms via Sequence-to-Function), a framework that trains supervised classifiers on multimodal variant effect predictions (ATAC-seq and RNA-seq) from the sequence-to-function model Borzoi and applies SHAP-based attribution to associate individual GWAS variants with the cell types most relevant to their disease association. Applied to asthma, LDL cholesterol, multiple sclerosis, and type 2 diabetes, GEMS prioritizes known disease-relevant cell types concordant with stratified LD-score regression. At the variant level, GEMS associates a median of 58.7% of fine-mapped variants with at least one cell type via ATAC-seq and 65.9% via RNA-seq, extending cellular annotation beyond the chromatin accessibility peaks in the single-cell atlas used for model training. ATAC-seq variant-cell-type associations are significantly enriched in cis-regulatory elements from independent experimental studies not used in model training, and enrichment persists after excluding variants overlapping training atlas peaks. For multiple sclerosis, hierarchical biclustering of variant--cell-type associations partitions risk variants into immune and CNS modules driven by distinct transcription factor families, recapitulating the immune-mediated and neurodegenerative components of the disease and demonstrating that integrative analysis of sequence-to-function predictions can stratify phenotype-associated variants into mechanistically distinct, cell-type-specific regulatory programs.

papers.abstract_full: AIMS: To evaluate whether a coronary artery disease (CAD) polygenic risk score (PRS) identifies clinically low-risk individuals at elevated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk. METHODS: We conducted a longitudinal cohort study within the UK Biobank including adults aged 40-74 years, free of ASCVD and diabetes, not on lipid-lowering therapy, and with baseline LDL <190 mg/dL. Participants were enrolled from 2006 to 2010 and followed through 2021. Ten-year ASCVD risk was estimated using pooled cohort equations. A CAD PRS derived from 2.3 million genome-wide variants was categorized as top 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, and bottom 50%. Lipoprotein(a) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein were similarly stratified. The primary endpoint was a composite of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or cardiovascular death. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for 10-year ASCVD events, and net reclassification improvement (NRI) was assessed at 5% and 7.5% risk thresholds. RESULTS: Among 266,917 low-risk individuals (median age 54; 38% male), ASCVD risk increased substantially across higher PRS strata. Compared with the bottom 50%, individuals in the top 50% had more than double the risk (aHR 2.48), the top 20% had over triple the risk (aHR 3.71), and the top 5% and 1% had 6-fold (aHR 6.31) and 9-fold (aHR 9.73) higher risks, respectively (all p < 0.0001). Adding PRS improved model discrimination (AUC 0.76 vs 0.72) and reclassified 12% of low-risk individuals upward-over tenfold more than Lp(a) or hs-CRP. CONCLUSION: In primary prevention, a CAD PRS identifies individuals with markedly higher ASCVD risk despite low clinical risk estimates and may merit consideration among ASCVD risk enhancers.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) results from the interplay between environmental and genetic factors. The relationship between sarcopenia index (SI) and VTE risk remains unclear. The combined effects of SI and genetic susceptibility on VTE risk have not been fully elucidated. We therefore investigated these associations using data from the UK Biobank. METHODS: Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess the relationship between SI and genetic susceptibility with incident VTE. Restricted cubic spline models were applied to examine the exposure-response relationships. RESULTS: Among 447,681 participants, 12,008 developed VTE during a median follow-up of 13.4 years. Higher SI was associated with a lower risk of VTE. The fully adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for Q2 to Q4 vs Q1 were 0.88 (95% CI, 0.83-0.92), 0.82 (95% CI, 0.78-0.87), and 0.77 (95% CI, 0.72-0.82), respectively. Restricted cubic spline analysis showed an inverse nonlinear association between SI and VTE (P for nonlinear <.001). Participants with high genetic risk had a higher risk of VTE (HR = 2.56; 95% CI, 2.42-2.72). Furthermore, participants with both low SI levels and high genetic susceptibility exhibited a significantly increased risk of VTE compared with those with high SI and low genetic risk (HR = 3.60; 95% CI, 3.14-4.12). CONCLUSION: Participants with lower SI had a significantly higher risk of VTE. Consistent with previous UK Biobank findings, higher polygenic risk score levels were associated with an increased risk of VTE. Moreover, participants with both low SI levels and high genetic risk exhibited the greatest risk of VTE. These findings suggest that SI may serve as a simple and accessible marker for identifying individuals at elevated risk of VTE.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and psychiatric disorders frequently co-occur; however, it remains unclear whether this overlap is generalized or defined by particular T2D mechanisms and psychiatric phenotypes. We investigated whether genetically defined T2D pathways show distinct associations with psychiatric and related phenotypes. METHODS: We calculated polygenic risk scores (PRSs) for 8 mechanistic T2D clusters and tested associations with psychiatric and sleep phenotypes and chronic pain in the UK Biobank. The study included 408,063 White British participants (54.1% female) and 50,214 non-overlapping White European participants (56.2% female). Models incorporated demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, anthropometric, and medication factors, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction across all tests. RESULTS: Adiposity PRS showed the broadest associations. Body-fat distribution PRS was associated with atypical major depressive disorder across all models, whereas obesity-mediated insulin-resistance PRS was associated only in the minimally adjusted model. Neither PRS was associated with nonatypical depression after FDR correction. Body-fat PRS was associated with generalized anxiety disorder, mood instability, long sleep duration, and chronic pain in all models. Associations for the other pathways were more selective and were concentrated in sleep duration and chronotype; metabolic-syndrome PRS was consistently associated with neuroticism. Cross-sample support was strongest for the association between obesity-mediated insulin-resistance PRS and morning chronotype. CONCLUSIONS: The overlap between T2D and psychiatric phenotypes was heterogeneous, with the strongest evidence for adiposity PRS and atypical depression and with more selective associations across other pathways. Considering heterogeneity in both T2D biology and psychiatric presentation may help clarify shared mechanisms. Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and psychiatric disorders frequently co-occur. T2D is heterogeneous, with different mechanisms contributing to disease development in different people. Genetic variation that represents 8 mechanisms of T2D has been identified. In the UK Biobank study, we used genetic data to estimate the 8 mechanisms and explored how these mechanisms influence psychiatric disorders and related traits (including sleep problems and chronic pain). We found that specific T2D mechanisms were related to specific features of psychiatric disorders and related traits. The body fat mechanism was associated with atypical depression, anxiety, and chronic pain. The other mechanisms mainly influenced sleep traits.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) may be associated with persistent subjective cognitive complaints, including difficulties with attention, memory, and executive function, in some individuals with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC, "long COVID"). Inter-individual variability raises the possibility that host genetic factors contribute to susceptibility. This study explored the relationship between dementia-related polygenic risk scores (PRS) and subjective cognitive burden after COVID-19. METHODS: Genome-wide genotype data from 60 individuals with a history of COVID-19 were merged with 915 South Asian population reference samples (total N = 975). Dementia-related PRS were generated using PRSice-2 across prespecified GWAS p-value thresholds. A subset of 15 participants completed a structured, study-specific self-report questionnaire assessing perceived cognitive difficulties across multiple domains 24-30 months after infection. Principal component analysis (PCA) summarized shared variance across cognitive domains. Associations between PRS and cognitive scores were examined using Spearman's rank correlation. All analyses were considered exploratory because no independent validation cohort was available. RESULTS: COVID-19-affected individuals aged 18-52 years showed a modest rightward shift in dementia-related PRS compared with population reference samples, with substantial overlap between groups (mean standardized PRS 0.24 vs. - 0.01; Mann-Whitney U = 29,504.5, p = 0.065; Cohen's d = 0.25). Memory-related difficulties contributed most strongly to the shared variance across cognitive domains, with PC1 explaining 52.5% of the variance. Among the 15 participants with cognitive assessment, PRS showed a positive but uncertain association with subjective cognitive burden (Spearman's r = 0.51, 95% CI - 0.02 to 0.82, p = 0.054). CONCLUSION: This hypothesis-generating study identified a possible relationship between dementia-related genetic liability and subjective cognitive burden after COVID-19. The PRS group comparison was descriptive and should not be interpreted as evidence of increased dementia risk. The phenotype-genotype finding is severely limited by the small subgroup, possible selection bias, non-validated subjective assessment, lack of multivariable adjustment, and cross-sectional design. Validation in larger, ancestry-matched, longitudinal cohorts is required.

papers.abstract_full: Major depressive disorder (MDD) susceptibility reflects both stable inherited liability and dynamic behavioral patterns, yet these dimensions are rarely examined together using long-term data in real-world settings. Here, we integrated genomic, electronic health record (EHR), and longitudinal Fitbit wearable data from 3030 adults of genetically inferred European ancestry in the All of Us Research Program, 284 of whom had an EHR-recorded MDD diagnosis during follow-up after a 180-day baseline period. Time-varying Cox models examined associations of the MDD polygenic score (PGS), monthly wearable-derived physical activity and sleep features, and wearable feature × MDD PGS interactions with EHR-recorded MDD. Higher MDD PGS, lower daily steps, lower light and vigorous physical activity, lower sleep efficiency, and greater sleep duration variability were associated with a higher hazard of EHR-recorded MDD. The associations of sedentary time and sleep duration variability with MDD differed across MDD PGS levels, with stronger associations among participants with higher MDD PGS. Model-estimated hazard ratio curves across MDD PGS levels further showed that the behavioral levels corresponding to the same relative hazard differed across levels of genetic liability, with more favorable behavioral levels observed at higher MDD PGS levels. Sequentially integrating MDD PGS, baseline wearable features, monthly wearable features, and selected wearable feature × MDD PGS interactions increased model discrimination, with the C-index increasing from 0.637 to 0.705. These findings support the complementary value of genetic liability and longitudinal behavioral monitoring for characterization of MDD susceptibility and may inform work on genetically informed digital phenotyping for personalized monitoring and prevention.

papers.abstract_full: Gene-environment correlations (rGE) present challenges for accurately estimating the individual and joint contributions of genetic and environmental influences on risk for psychiatric and substance use disorders. The present study examined rGE between polygenic risk scores (PGS) for psychiatric and substance use disorders and environmental exposures (i.e., exposome factors) using multi-level data spanning youth- and parent-reports, as well as objective measures of the built environment. Participants included 4,797 genetically similar to European reference populations, 1,585 genetically similar to African reference populations, and 2,012 genetically similar to Admixed American reference populations from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. The ABCD study was conducted at 21 sites across the U.S and used a stratified probability sampling design to ensure the cohort recruited was demographically diverse. Based on factor-analytic work conducted by Moore et al. (2022) in the ABCD study, the exposome included 6 factors: household adversity, neighborhood adversity, positive day-to-day experiences, state conservatism/ruralness, family values, and pregnancy/birth complications. Disorder-specific PGS for psychiatric (e.g., major depressive disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) and substance use conditions (e.g., alcohol use disorders, cannabis use disorders), as well as PGS for common liability for externalizing and general substance use disorders, were used to examine genetic associations with the exposome factors. After adjusting for participant sex, age, log income-to-needs ratio, and genetic ancestry principal components, higher PGS for psychiatric (e.g., broad externalizing liability, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) and substance use disorders (e.g., general substance use disorders, cannabis use disorder) were positively associated with household adversity and negatively associated with positive day-to-day experiences. Our results indicate that polygenic risk for psychiatric and substance use disorders correlate with environmental factors in adolescence at multiple levels, most notably household adversity and positive day-to-day experiences. Findings underscore the importance of investigating rGE when examining these environmental exposures with genetic risk for psychiatric and substance use disorders.
