papers.title: Cross-trait genetic architecture of intracerebral hemorrhage highlights convergent vascular, hematologic and lipid pathways.
papers.abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a severe stroke subtype, but the extent to which its susceptibility architecture is shared with other complex traits remains unclear. Here we integrated FinnGen release 12 ICH summary statistics (5112 cases and 450,016 controls) with 898 GWAS datasets curated through BIGA and the GWAS Catalog, and applied a layered analytical framework spanning linkage disequilibrium score regression, cross-trait association testing, locus annotation, Bayesian colocalization, mu…
papers.abstract_full: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a severe stroke subtype, but the extent to which its susceptibility architecture is shared with other complex traits remains unclear. Here we integrated FinnGen release 12 ICH summary statistics (5112 cases and 450,016 controls) with 898 GWAS datasets curated through BIGA and the GWAS Catalog, and applied a layered analytical framework spanning linkage disequilibrium score regression, cross-trait association testing, locus annotation, Bayesian colocalization, multi-method gene prioritization, and two-sample Mendelian randomization. Among 46 nominal LDSC correlations (P < 0.05), only stroke and one atrial-fibrillation dataset remained significant after both Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate and Bonferroni correction; the hematologic and fatty-acid/lipid correlations were therefore treated as exploratory. Joint analyses yielded 34 MTAG-positive and 45 CPASSOC-positive trait pairs, whereas locus-level refinement highlighted recurrent regions at 1q22, 2q33, 5p15.33, 13q34, and 15q, with 15 regions showing evidence of colocalization (PP.H4 > 0.7). Integrative prioritization across SMR, FUSION, mBAT-combo, and PoPS nominated 117 candidate genes, including ten genes supported by all four approaches, with EHD4, ICA1L, NBEAL1, FAM117B, SH3PXD2A, CARF, SRR, HIC1, TLR6, and FAM114A1 forming the highest-confidence set. Bidirectional Mendelian randomization identified seven FDR-supported trait-to-ICH associations involving atrial fibrillation, small-vessel stroke, erythrocyte indices, fatty-acid traits, and a clinical-treatment phenotype. No ICH-to-trait association survived multiple-testing correction, and the variable sensitivity support indicated that these findings should be interpreted as exploratory directional evidence rather than established causal effects. Together, these analyses position ICH within a broader cross-trait genetic network centered on cerebral small-vessel vulnerability, blood-cell homeostasis, and lipid composition, and provide a prioritized framework for downstream mechanistic and functional studies.

papers.abstract_full: This study investigated the pleiotropy and the underlying biology linking COVID-19 outcomes to brain variation, leveraging genome-wide data from the COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative and multimodal brain-wide magnetic resonance imaging from the UK Biobank. In our analyses, COVID-19 outcomes showed evidence of polygenic overlap with respect to 11 imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) related to brain structure (e.g. parahippocampal and entorhinal cortical thickness) and connectivity (e.g. Broca's area and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex). Among these, the genetic liability to COVID-19 hospitalization and SARS-CoV-2 infection was inversely related to the area of pars opercularis. We also identified local genetic correlations between COVID-19 outcomes and brain IDPs within five loci mapping genes involved in inflammatory response, immune regulation, brain development, and neuropsychiatric disorders (e.g. LAMP3, SOX2, and TSHZ2). Additionally, we uncovered colocalized variants linking COVID-19 outcomes to brain structural variation (rs13107325 with entorhinal mean thickness) and brain transcriptomic regulation of immune-related genes (e.g. IL6R in brain cortex and HLA-C in caudate basal ganglia). Our drug-repurposing analysis based on gene ontologies shared between COVID-19 outcomes and brain IDPs uncovered 41 compounds, including psychiatric medications that appear to also have antiviral and immunomodulatory activity. Overall, the present findings contributed to dissecting the biological mechanisms shared between COVID-19 and brain variation, highlighting the systemic nature of their relationship.

papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has been associated with subclinical myocardial inflammation. Post-COVID-19 infection, there are concerns about subsequent heart failure and persistent myocarditis. It is unknown how COVID-19 infection compares with non-COVID-19 viral infections in terms of myocardial inflammation based on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) assessment. This prospective longitudinal study aims to determine and compare the extent and severity of myocardial involvement in patients with COVID-19 infection versus non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infections (control). METHOD: Recruited recovered COVID-19 (RCOVID) patients and recovered non-COVID (non-COVID) patients from several hospitals and COVID-19-designated clinic underwent three CMR examinations for functional assessment, native T1, T2, and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification, with corroborating blood markers (NT-proBNP, white cell count, c-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and high sensitivity cardiac troponin T). CMR scans took place (i) within 2-week of confirmed recovery, (ii) 3-month, and (iii) 12-month post-recovery. Linear mixed model with Bonferroni correction was used for analysis. RESULTS: 152 participants were recruited, 112 RCOVID outpatients (mean age: 41.0; 58.9% female) and 40 non-COVID inpatients (mean age:45.0; 37.5% female). Non-COVID infections included influenza virus, rhinovirus/enterovirus, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus. At all three time points, blood results and cardiac function parameters were not significantly different between RCOVID and non-COVID patient groups (p-value not significant). Both patient groups had no significant differences for native T1/T2 values, ECV, late gadolinium enhancement, T2 short tau inversion recovery, and overall fulfilment of the 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria at each time points. CONCLUSION: In this prospective longitudinal study with CMR examinations, COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse myocardial inflammatory response than non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infection in terms of CMR parameters, and blood markers. PLAIN ENGLISH SUMMARY: During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreaks, some COVID-19 patients were incidentally found to have inflammation of the muscular layer of the heart. Healthcare professionals were concerned the inflammation will lead to heart not delivering enough blood to meet body demands (ie. heart failure) in the long run. Therefore, we designed this study to better understand the extent and severity of cardiac involvement in patients with COVID-19 by comparing them to patients with other types of viral respiratory infections, such as influenza, which we were more familiar with. We recruited two groups of patients, one group with patients recovered from COVID-19, the other group with patients recovered from other types of viral respiratory infections. For each patient, we arranged three assessments at 2 weeks, 3 months, and 12 months after their recovery respectively. During each assessment, they had blood taken and underwent a cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) scan, a type of medical imaging used for assessment of heart function. 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria (LLC) is a set of criteria for diagnosis of myocardial inflammation recommended by a group of experts. We compared the two groups of patients at each time point according to LLC, as well as their blood markers and heart function. In our study, we found that COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse heart muscle inflammatory response than other types of viral respiratory infections. This is reassuring as patients with previous COVID-19 infections will likely not develop inflammation of the heart muscle nor develop heart failure.

papers.abstract_full: Elucidating the metabolic regulatory mechanisms underlying meat production traits in broilers is essential to overcome the limitations of traditional breeding methods and to achieve precise genetic improvement. This study systematically investigated the metabolic basis of meat production traits and screened metabolic biomarkers suitable for selective breeding to enhance these traits. A total of 441 birds from Northeast Agricultural University broiler lines that were divergently selected for abdominal fat content were used as experimental material. Genetic parameters for body weight, abdominal fat content, and key meat production traits were estimated, followed by plasma non-targeted metabolomic analysis. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to construct metabolite co-expression modules. Modules significantly correlated with pectoralis muscle and leg muscle ratios were identified, together with the corresponding enriched pathways. Additionally, hub metabolites were screened based on module membership (|MM| > 0.8) and gene significance (|GS| > 0.6), and their heritability and genetic correlations with meat production traits were estimated to identify potential metabolic markers. Genetic analysis revealed that, despite no significant difference in body weight at 7 weeks between the lean line (high-feed‑efficiency birds) and the fat line (low-feed‑efficiency birds), abdominal fat and key meat production traits showed significant divergence. Meat production traits demonstrated moderate to high heritability (h² ≥ 0.2). WGCNA identified metabolic modules associated with meat production traits, including tyrosine metabolism (brown module), amino acid biosynthesis (turquoise module), and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis (turquoise module) in both sexes. Additionally, in females, sulfur metabolism and unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis (blue module) were also associated with meat production traits. Using stringent thresholds (|MM| > 0.8, |GS| > 0.6), 39 hub metabolites were screened (18 in males, 30 in females). Further evaluation integrating heritability and genetic correlation identified 11 candidate metabolic markers with moderate-to-high heritability (h² ≥ 0.2) and strong genetic correlation (rg ≥ 0.4) with meat production traits, including Engelhardione, LPC(18:1), LysoPE(20:4), isocitrate, and l-lysine. These findings indicate that pathways related to tyrosine metabolism and amino acid biosynthesis play important roles in meat production traits, and that 11 metabolic markers identified through the integration of WGCNA and genetic parameter analysis may support breeding strategies to enhance meat yield.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: The role of lipid-lowering therapies (e.g., statins) during anticoagulation for Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) remains unclear. This study investigated the causal role of lipid traits in VTE and evaluated lipid-lowering drug targets using a Mendelian Randomization (MR) approach. METHODS: Genetic variants associated with lipid traits and lipid-lowering drug targets were extracted from the Global Lipids Genetics Consortium GWAS. Summary statistics for VTE, Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), and Pulmonary Embolism (PE) were obtained from UK Biobank. For associated targets, expression quantitative trait loci data were analyzed using summary-data-based MR. Colocalization analysis assessed shared genetic signals, and molecular docking explored plausible ligand-target binding poses. RESULTS: Higher triglyceride levels were associated with lower VTE (OR = 0.998, 95% CI: 0.996‒1.000, p = 0.035) and DVT risks (OR = 0.998, 95% CI: 0.997‒1.000, p = 0.012). Genetic mimicry of Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL) enhancement was nominally associated with lower VTE odds (OR = 0.997, 95% CI: 0.995‒1.000, p = 0.02) and with lower PE odds after Bonferroni correction (OR = 0.996, 95% CI: 0.994‒0.998, p = 5.29E-06), but not DVT. LPL expression in whole blood showed a significant MR association with PE (OR = 1.001, 95% CI: 1.000‒1.002, p = 0.039) and moderate colocalization (PP.H4 = 0.68). Molecular docking predicted plausible active-site or allosteric binding poses for three LPL agonists (binding energies ≤ -6.8 kcal/mol). CONCLUSIONS: Genetically proxied LPL enhancement was nominally associated with modestly lower composite VTE risk and was associated with lower PE risk after multiple-testing correction, although no association was observed for DVT. These findings support a potential role for LPL-related pathways in VTE biology and warrant independent genetic and functional validation before clinical translation.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) is a leading cause of mortality worldwide and comprises multiple clinical phenotypes, but their shared genetic architecture remains incompletely defined. METHODS: We integrated genome-wide association study summary statistics for coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, large-artery atherosclerotic stroke, and carotid plaque using genomic structural equation modeling to derive a multivariable ASCVD common factor. We applied fine-mapping, multi-marker analysis of genomic annotation, transcriptome-wide association studies, Mendelian randomization, colocalization, mediation analysis, and virtual screening. RESULTS: We identified 289 linkage disequilibrium-independent lead single-nucleotide polymorphisms mapping to 177 genomic risk loci; 13 lacked corresponding genome-wide significant signals in the input genome-wide association studies. Eleven had prior genome-wide association study catalog association records, whereas no relevant records were identified for the loci represented by rs2294777 near SASH1 and rs4843053 near AKAP13. Fine-mapping prioritized 26 putative causal variants. Integrated functional summary-based imputation, multi-tissue transcriptome-wide association study, and multi-marker analysis of genomic annotation analyses implicated 123 genes. Enrichment analyses highlighted endothelial cells and H3K27ac-marked regulatory regions. Lipidomic analyses linked higher triacylglycerols and sterol esters to increased multivariable ASCVD common factor risk. Protein Mendelian randomization analyses in deCODE and Fenland prioritized aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), phosphodiesterase 5A (PDE5A), HtrAserinepeptidase 1 (HTRA1), and transcription elongation factor A2 (TCEA2) as candidate targets. Colocalization supported a shared causal variant between TCEA2 and multivariable ASCVD common factor. Mediation analyses suggested partial mediation by diastolic blood pressure for ALDH2, PDE5A, and TCEA2 and by triglycerides for TCEA2. Virtual screening identified candidate compounds with favorable predicted binding to PDE5A and ALDH2. CONCLUSIONS: Integrating multivariate genome-wide association study with multi-omics and causal inference analyses identified shared genetic signals associated with ASCVD susceptibility and prioritized candidate protein targets, informing future functional studies and target validation.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Influenza remains a significant global health burden, potentially leading to hospitalization and mortality. Although previous studies have explored genetic susceptibility to influenza infection, the genetic basis of influenza hospitalization and its relationship with respiratory diseases like COVID-19 remain poorly understood. METHODS: We performed a binary GWAS of hospitalized influenza using UK Biobank data (UKBB; 1037 cases/404,108 controls) and then meta-analyzed results with the FinnGen GWAS, yielding 11,171 cases and 782,400 controls. A time-to-event GWAS in UKBB was also performed to identify genetic factors underlying the timing (age) of first influenza hospitalization. p-values from both analyses were integrated by the harmonic mean p-value (HMP) method to enhance association detection. Further differentiation and colocalization analyses with COVID-19 investigated their distinct and shared genetic features. An integrative framework combining functional annotations, multi-omics analyses, and phenome-wide scans prioritized key risk and differential genes. RESULTS: The binary GWAS meta-analysis identified three loci (ST6GAL1, AASDHPPT, SPATS2L) associated with hospitalization risk. The time-to-event GWAS recognized UGT2B4 as linked to hospitalization timing. HMP analysis, which combines evidence across the binary and time-to-event analyses, identified ST6GAL1 (p = 3 × 10-9) and UGT2B4 (p = 3.63 × 10-8) as genome-wide significant; however, each signal was driven predominantly by one component test, ST6GAL1 by the binary meta-analysis (meta p = 1.5 × 10-9), and UGT2B4 by the time-to-event analysis (SPACox p = 1.82 × 10-8), rather than showing independent support from both analyses. Differentiation analysis identified 29 loci and two tissues distinguishing influenza from COVID-19, whereas analysis of shared association signals (cofdr) highlighted candidate shared genetic factors, including ST6GAL1 and ICAM5 (gene-level PPA ≥ 0.9). CONCLUSIONS: This study uncovers the genetic architectures of hospitalized influenza. It also highlights genetic differences and similarities with COVID-19, providing hypothesis-generating insights that may inform future functional and therapeutic research.

papers.title: Managing Trait Trade-Offs in Tomato Breeding Through Genome Editing.
papers.abstract: Tomato improvement often involves trade-offs between fruit yield and quality, sweetness and fruit size, disease resistance and growth, reproductive performance and stress adaptation, and shelf life and flavour. Although CRISPR-Cas-mediated genome editing enables targeted modification of tomato genes, DNA-level precision does not guarantee an agronomically favourable phenotype because pleiotropy, functional redundancy, allele dosage, linkage, epistasis, genetic background, and environmental condi…
papers.abstract_full: Tomato improvement often involves trade-offs between fruit yield and quality, sweetness and fruit size, disease resistance and growth, reproductive performance and stress adaptation, and shelf life and flavour. Although CRISPR-Cas-mediated genome editing enables targeted modification of tomato genes, DNA-level precision does not guarantee an agronomically favourable phenotype because pleiotropy, functional redundancy, allele dosage, linkage, epistasis, genetic background, and environmental conditions can alter editing outcomes. This review evaluates genome editing as a strategy to manage, rather than merely document, these trade-offs. We examine how knockout, multiplex, cis-regulatory, base, prime, and direct allele-repair approaches can match the causal architecture of a breeding constraint. We critically assess representative studies involving plant architecture, reproductive development, fruit size, sugar accumulation, ripening, nutritional composition, disease resistance, and heat resilience, with an emphasis on heritability, molecular identity, multi-trait effects, and agronomic penalties. We further consider domestication-associated variation, structural variation, transformation and regeneration limitations, genotype-by-environment interactions, breeding deployment, and regulatory translation. We propose a trade-off-aware framework that links causal-allele identification, mechanism-matched editing, quantitative allele design, multidimensional phenotyping, and validation across generations, genetic backgrounds, and production-relevant environments. This framework can guide the development of balanced, breeding-ready tomato cultivars rather than lines optimized for a single trait.

papers.abstract_full: Heat stress adversely affects porcine reproduction, but genetic variation in the response of age at puberty (AP) to heat exposure remains poorly characterized in gilts. We analyzed 4438 AP records from Yorkshire gilts using adjusted meteorological data and compared three heat-exposure gradients across five prepubertal windows. Pedigree- and single-step genomic reaction-norm models were fitted, followed by single-step genome-wide association analyses of the intercept and slope. Among the 15 exposure scenarios, the best-fitting model used the proportion of sustained heat-stress days in the 14-day window before first observed estrus; a one-standard-deviation increase in this measure was associated with a 7.64-day increase in AP. Both reaction-norm models detected significant genetic variance for environmental sensitivity (p < 0.001). The genomic intercept-slope genetic correlation was -0.524, and genetic variances and correlations varied across the exposure gradient. GEBVs rankings at the 10th and 90th percentiles of the exposure gradient were negatively correlated (Spearman's ρ = -0.742), and the most favorable 10% of gilts did not overlap between these two exposure levels. Intercept and slope window contributions were strongly correlated (Spearman's ρ = 0.822), although component-specific regions were also detected. Functional annotation highlighted candidate genes and biological processes related to neuroendocrine regulation, ovarian development, mitochondrial and redox homeostasis, and cellular stress responses. These findings reveal genetically heterogeneous heat sensitivity in AP, supporting environment-specific genomic evaluation for reproductive robustness in gilts.

papers.abstract_full: This study characterized the genetic basis of reproductive and calving traits in Jersey cattle at different physiological stages and identified potential candidate genes. After quality control, 2716 records were available for heifer reproductive traits, 2707 for multiparous cow reproductive traits, and 5423 calving records for calving ease (CE) and calf birth weight (CBW). CE and CBW were analyzed from the maternal perspective, with records assigned to the corresponding dams. Genetic parameters were estimated using AI-REML in DMU with animal, repeatability, and bivariate models. Genome-wide association analyses were performed using a mixed linear model based on 1,660,477 SNPs from 1578 genotyped Jersey cattle. Heritability estimates for age at first service (AFS) and age at first calving (AFC) were 0.416 and 0.380, respectively, whereas estimates for reproductive traits in multiparous cows were generally low (0.072-0.154). Calving interval (CI) and days open (DO) showed a strong positive genetic correlation (0.781). GWAS identified five significant loci associated with AFC, number of services per conception in heifers, CI, and dam-associated genetic variation in CE. Candidate genes included PIK3C2G, DGKI, ABCC1, CCDC85A, CRMP1, EVC, and EVC2. Exploratory KEGG enrichment suggested potential involvement of phosphatidylinositol signaling, Hedgehog signaling, ABC transporters, and inositol phosphate metabolism. Overall, reproductive traits showed distinct genetic characteristics between heifers and multiparous cows, and AFS and AFC exhibited relatively greater potential for genetic improvement. The identified genomic regions provide preliminary candidates for further validation and potential future application in genomic breeding.

papers.abstract_full: Purpose: Volumetric PET biomarkers carry substantial prognostic value in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet their clinical implementation is hampered by segmentation heterogeneity. A fundamental and unresolved question is which segmentation method is most suitable for routine clinical use, both for a reader experienced in PET segmentation and for a reader without PET segmentation experience, such as an ENT surgeon or a radiation oncologist. This study addressed this question by assessing the intra- and interobserver reproducibility of four PET segmentation methods in MIM Maestro Software Version 7.4.2, identifying tumour-related determinants of variability, and examining concordance between PET-derived metabolic tumour volume (MTV) and CT-based gross tumour volume (GTV). Methods: Two readers with contrasting PET segmentation experience, a nuclear medicine physician experienced in PET segmentation (R1) and an ENT surgeon without prior PET segmentation training (R2), applied four methods to the primary tumours of 154 patients with HNSCC (oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx or larynx) treated with definitive (chemo)radiotherapy between 2010 and 2021: fixed absolute thresholds at SUV 3.0 and 4.0, a relative threshold at 41% of the maximum standardised uptake value (SUVmax), and a gradient edge-detection algorithm (PET Edge+). R1 segmented twice with a washout of at least 4 weeks; R2 performed one session and delineated CT-GTV in the 85 patients whose PET/CT-derived CT served directly as the radiotherapy planning scan. The second session of R1 served as the reference for all interobserver and MTV-GTV analyses. Agreement was assessed by ICC (two-way mixed model), coefficient of variation, repeatability coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis; determinants of variability by a multivariable linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept per patient. Results: All four methods demonstrated excellent intraobserver (ICC 0.993 to >0.999) and interobserver (ICC 0.989-0.996) reproducibility. SUV3.0 generated significantly more relative error than SUV41% (β = +3.1%; 95% CI 0.89, 5.3). PET Edge+ was the only method for which a significant method × reader interaction was observed in this reader pair: the reader without PET segmentation experience generated more error than the reader experienced in PET segmentation (β = +7.1%; 95% CI 3.9, 10), an effect concentrated in smaller tumours (below approximately 15 mL); in the 85-patient GTV subset, where tumours were larger on average, the interobserver ICC for PET Edge+ was 0.997. GTV concordance was good for three of four methods (ICC 0.808-0.895); SUV41% showed only moderate concordance (ICC 0.572). Conclusions: All four methods provided excellent volumetric reproducibility within a single clinical software platform, but they differed in reader dependence and in agreement with CT-defined GTV. Rather than supporting a universal segmentation standard, these findings suggest that the method should be selected according to its intended application, pending multicentre confirmation.

papers.abstract_full: Background/Objectives: Diabetic cardiomyopathy is an under-recognized complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), often co-existing with diabetic nephropathy. This study investigates whether patients with T1DM and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) undergoing simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplantation (SPKT) show echocardiographic signs of cardiomyopathy prior to surgery and explores whether cardiac changes are more attributable to diabetes itself or to chronic kidney disease. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed preoperative echocardiographic data of 16 SPKT patients with T1DM and ESRD, using 2D speckle tracking for strain assessment. Data were compared to individually matched control groups: (1) ESRD patients without diabetes (n = 20) and (2) healthy controls (n = 48). Left and right ventricular/atrial function and structure were analyzed, including 2D speckle-tracking analysis. A mixed-effects model adjusted for age, sex, coronary artery disease, and hypertension. Results: SPKT patients exhibited significant structural changes in the left heart, including increased left ventricular mass and left atrial volume index, alongside reduced global longitudinal strain (GLS), global radial strain (GRS), and global circumferential strain (GCS) compared to healthy controls. GRS and GCS were significantly lower in the SPKT group than in the ESRD group without diabetes. Left atrial strain and strain rates were reduced in both disease groups. Right ventricular and atrial strain parameters did not significantly differ between groups. Mixed model analysis confirmed significant strain differences in the left ventricle even after adjusting for confounders. Conclusions: T1DM patients with end-stage nephropathy awaiting SPKT show echocardiographic abnormalities compatible with subclinical myocardial dysfunction, with predominant involvement of the left heart. Compared to non-diabetic ESRD patients, the diabetic cohort exhibited greater impairment in left ventricular strain parameters, supporting a pathophysiologic role of diabetes independent of kidney disease. Speckle-tracking analysis demonstrated potential utility for detecting early signs of myocardial dysfunction in this high-risk population.

papers.abstract: Within-field diversification, notably through cereal legume intercropping, is a major lever of the agroecological transition. Breeding cultivars adapted to intercropping requires major changes in breeding practices, owing to strong genotype-by-stand-type interactions and the high spatial heterogeneity of low-input field trials. papers.abstract_full: Within-field diversification, notably through cereal legume intercropping, is a major lever of the agroecological transition. Breeding cultivars adapted to intercropping requires major changes in breeding practices, owing to strong genotype-by-stand-type interactions and the high spatial heterogeneity of low-input field trials. Part of this heterogeneity stems from variation in plant density, a first yield component that strongly influences resource competition and is critical to monitor in intercrops. Given the many plots in such platforms, high-throughput phenotyping of plant density is essential. Over two seasons, we designed a large field trial involving 200 wheat cultivars observed as sole crop as well as intercropped with two pea tester cultivars, in a pseudo-randomized complete block design. Plant density was manually counted on 40 cultivars, alongwith UAV flights at both high and low altitudes. We propose a method to predict plant density from millimeter-resolution RGB images, using linear regression on log-transformed fractional vegetation cover and additional colorimetric and textural indices. We predict total density of wheat or pea in sole crops, or the combined pea+wheat total density in intercrops with relative RMSE of 19.2% and 27.4% depending on season. Thanks to the pipeline, total plant density was predicted across the entire trial, comprising more than 1,000 microplots (200 varieties); this density showed high heritability (0.75-0.85). We provide guidelines regarding the composition of the training set for such intercrop trials. High-throughput phenotyping approaches such as the one proposed here can be instrumental in mobilizing genetic diversity for agroecology.

papers.abstract_full: The mechanisation of agriculture has achieved major increases in labour productivity but has also led to an erosion of agrobiodiversity. Neglected and underutilized crops such as common buckwheat (  Fagopyrum esculentum Moench) offer the potential to diversify food production systems but require major genetic improvement to compete with established crops. Although target traits for breeding such as more homogeneous ripening, reduced height, larger seeds and higher and more stable yields are well known, large-scale and field-based phenotyping data of diverse common buckwheat accessions across multiple environments are still scarce. Here, we tested the agronomic performance of a common buckwheat germplasm collection consisting of 170 accessions of diverse origin. The collection was tested at seven year-sites, and 19 agronomic traits related to phenology, growth habit and yield were assessed. Most traits showed high repeatability (0.31 < R  2 < 0.98) and heritability (0.45 < H  2 < 0.97), indicating genetic control of these traits. Coefficients of variation ranged between 6.19% and 46.15%, showing the high phenotypic diversity within the collection. By combining multiple traits, distinct ideotypes for different roles in the crop rotation were investigated, and accessions with promising agronomic profiles identified. Genome-wide association studies revealed marker-trait associations for 18 traits, allowing the identification of putative candidate genes influencing these traits such as a putative  GRF-INTERACTING FACTOR associated with flowering time and biomass production. Our results show that the collection offers vast phenotypic diversity that can be exploited for the development of improved varieties tailored to meet specific agronomic purposes. The efficient utilization of these genetic resources should be supported by the application of genomics-based breeding approaches. The development of genetic markers and search for putative candidate genes mark important steps towards the establishment of efficient breeding schemes. Thus, these genomic resources provide a foundation for accelerating the genetic improvement of common buckwheat and developing agronomically competitive varieties.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT  The objective of this study was to perform a systematic review and multi-level meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for functional traits in dairy cattle, focusing on calving performance and udder health. papers.abstract_full: ABSTRACT  The objective of this study was to perform a systematic review and multi-level meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for functional traits in dairy cattle, focusing on calving performance and udder health. We hypothesized that despite the limited replication of individual SNPs across independent studies, functionally related variants would converge on common genes, biological pathways, and genomic regions. Following a systematic literature search and a two-stage filtering process, we extracted data from 20 independent articles covering seven traits: direct and maternal calving ease, direct and maternal stillbirth, clinical mastitis, somatic cell count, and somatic cell score. We first conducted a conventional SNP-level meta-analysis, which demonstrated minimal variant overlap across studies, preventing the detection of significant pooled effects. To resolve this low overlap, we mapped the associated variants to higher organizational levels, including genes, proteins, KEGG and Reactome pathways, and quantitative trait loci (QTL), and combined the statistical evidence using Fisher’s method. This multi-level functional mapping revealed significant biological convergence. At the gene level, we identified shared genes such as CCDC170 linking maternal calving ease and maternal stillbirth, while DCK, TMPRSS11F, and SLC4A4 were significant for udder health traits. Pathway-level meta-analysis highlighted major functional networks, demonstrating that mastitis-related traits were strongly associated with immune response, signal transduction, and cellular stress pathways, whereas maternal calving traits were dominated by endocrine and calcium signaling. Furthermore, our cross-trait overlap analysis identified 35 shared pathways and 30 shared QTL, reflecting a common biological architecture connecting calving difficulties and mastitis susceptibility. Notably, the innate immune system and signal transduction pathways consistently overlapped across multiple functional traits. In conclusion, conventional SNP-level meta-analysis has limited utility for integrating dairy cattle GWAS due to insufficient cross-study marker overlap. Moving from individual variants toward higher-order functional units effectively reveals reproducible genetic signals and functional convergence. The identified genes, biological pathways, and genomic regions offer valuable insights that can be leveraged as biological priors to improve genomic prediction models for dairy cattle health and reproduction. Interpretive summary  Genetic studies on dairy cattle health and calving traits often show limited replication of individual variants across independent populations. This study addresses this limitation by moving beyond conventional single-marker meta-analysis and integrating genome-wide association data at higher levels of biological organization: genes, proteins, pathways, and quantitative trait loci. By mapping variants from 20 independent studies to these higher-order functional units, we revealed a shared biological architecture  - such as immune and calcium signaling  - linking calving difficulties with mastitis susceptibility. These findings provide biological priors that can enhance genomic prediction models and breeding programs for dairy cattle functional traits.

papers.abstract_full: Trifluoroacetate (TFA) is an ultra-short chain perfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) and a pollutant of global significance; it is persistent and ubiquitous in the environment across compartments, including food, drinking water, animals, and humans. Concentrations in the environment are rising, concerns over the toxicity of the compound are increasing, and there are currently no efficient ways to remediate TFA pollution, as conventional methods are ineffective at scale under environmental conditions. Microorganisms possessing dehalogenating enzymes targeting the structurally analogous compound monofluoroacetate (MFA) present a potential solution to degrade TFA microbiologically. Due to previously demonstrated dehalogenation of difluoroacetate (DFA) by dehalogenases, the promiscuity of such enzymes was hypothesized to be extendable to TFA as well. In this study cultures obtained from an environmental sample of PFAS contaminated wastewater sludge were incubated in M9 minimal media supplied with 33 mM acetate and either 33 mM TFA, DFA, or MFA in an iterative manner, followed by testing in a 30-day experiment. Free fluoride (F  - ) was measured at 5 timepoints using a fluoride ion specific electrode (ISE).  One culture designated MFA1C significantly degraded MFA, DFA, and TFA (two-way ANOVA mixed model, p < 0.05). MFA1C released 11.2 ± 0.7 µM F  - which constitutes approximately 0.01% of the potential fluoride release from the total 33 mM TFA applied and with the greatest defluorination activity in the first 9 days of incubation. Fluoride release from TFA and formation of DFA and MFA was confirmed with  19 F-NMR. Genetic sequencing and protein-ligand modelling identified two candidate dehalogenase enzymes from  Achromobacter denitrificans and  Stenotrophomonas sp., respectively, with potential capacity to degrade TFA. The findings of this study are a crucial first step towards future potential bioremediation of TFA, and are, to the best of our knowledge, the first to identify a TFA-degrading consortium of microorganisms.

papers.abstract_full: Background:  & Aims: The intestinal epithelium renews continuously through cell cycle-dependent turnover, yet it remains unknown whether core cell cycle regulators directly control intestinal barrier function. We investigated how loss of the Cyclin E1/Cyclin E2/CDK2 complex affects intestinal homeostasis. Based on the important role of this complex in compensatory liver regeneration, we hypothesized that its combined loss would impair epithelial renewal and barrier integrity.  Methods: : We generated  Ccne2 −/− mice and triple knockout (TKO) mice with intestinal epithelial cell (IEC)-specific deletion of  Ccne1 and  Cdk2 on a constitutive  Ccne2 -null background and characterized intestinal architecture, proliferation, and barrier function using histology, immunoblotting, qPCR, and FITC-dextran permeability assays. Mechanistic findings were validated in CRISPR/Cas9-generated  Ccne2 -deficient and CDK1-overexpressing MC38 colon carcinoma cells using transcriptomics and kinomics approaches.  Results: : Contrary to our hypothesis, TKO maintained and  Ccne2 −/− mice even enhanced cell cycle activity selectively in the colon, along with enhanced  Cdk1 expression, had significantly lower serum FITC-dextran levels after oral administration, and increased  Tjp1 /ZO-1 expression, consistent with reduced intestinal permeability.  Ccne2 -deficient MC38 cells recapitulated the increase in ZO-1 and exhibited transcriptional enrichment of gene sets associated with tight junctions and cell cycle. CDK1 overexpression in MC38 cells increased ZO-1 protein abundance and was associated with activation of an AMPK-related kinase network. In TKO and  Ccne2 −/− colonic epithelium, CDK1, phosphorylated AMPK and ZO-1 showed partial colocalization at lateral epithelial cell-cell contacts.  Conclusions: : Loss of Cyclin E2, either alone or in combination with epithelial Cyclin E1/CDK2 deficiency, is associated with increased CDK1 expression and strengthens the colonic barrier integrity in mice. Findings from MC38 cells suggest that transcriptional reprogramming and enhanced CDK1 signaling in the context of Cyclin E2 deficiency may contribute to tight junction reinforcement and improved barrier function.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occurs with distinct personality profiles, but whether ADHD shapes personality (scar model) or personality influences the development of ADHD (vulnerability model) remains unclear. Leveraging genome-wide association study (GWAS) data, we examined directional associations between ADHD and the Big Five personality traits (Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness). We estimated genetic correlations and conducted bidirectional two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR) analyses between ADHD and the Big Five. Robustness was evaluated using multiple sensitivity tests, including MR-CAUSE, which accounts for correlated and uncorrelated pleiotropy, and colocalization analyses on fine-mapped variants. Higher genetic liability to Neuroticism and Extraversion, alongside lower liability to Conscientiousness, increased ADHD risk, consistent with the vulnerability model. Conversely, ADHD genetic liability was associated with lower Agreeableness, supporting the scar model. Associations were generally robust across sensitivity analyses, with MR-CAUSE supporting the Neuroticism and Agreeableness associations and colocalization providing variant-level support for associations between ADHD and Neuroticism, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness. These findings provide early, population-level insight into personality-related vulnerability to ADHD and motivate further work on the role of personality traits in ADHD risk.

papers.abstract: Abstract    Background  Whether the epigenome constitutes a "code" has been debated for a quarter-century, largely qualitatively. We make the question measurable by defining an epigenetic layer’s  codeness  as the geometric mean of three axes — heritability, causality and sequence-predictability — with heritability estimated as the mutual information a mark’s daughter-cell state carries about its mother-cell state conditional on DNA sequence, separating genuine self-templating from sequence-driv…
papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Background  Whether the epigenome constitutes a "code" has been debated for a quarter-century, largely qualitatively. We make the question measurable by defining an epigenetic layer’s  codeness  as the geometric mean of three axes — heritability, causality and sequence-predictability — with heritability estimated as the mutual information a mark’s daughter-cell state carries about its mother-cell state conditional on DNA sequence, separating genuine self-templating from sequence-driven re-derivation. Methods  We built a Monte-Carlo engine that parameterizes each axis from published perturbation and sequence-prediction data, and reanalyzed two primary datasets to ground the two load-bearing axes: Hammer-seq DNA-methylation inheritance and the genome-wide CRISPRoff transcriptional-memory screen. Results  Across seven mammalian layers the index resolves two mechanistic tiers — self-templating codes (DNA methylation, repressive marks, CENP-A) and sequence echoes (chromatin accessibility, active marks, most non-coding RNA). DNA methylation is the most code-like layer, whereas the most sequence-predictable layer is among the least code-like, so codeness is not predictability. Genome-wide methylation-inheritance mutual information is 0.72, and readability predicts CRISPRoff memory with a cross-validated AUC of 0.71. The index extends across bacteria, fungi, plants, invertebrates and mammals, where it suggests a separable "universal epigenetic codeness law" — a conserved layer ranking rescaled by a per-kingdom gain, broken only by carrier switches — which we advance as a falsifiable hypothesis. Conclusions  Codeness is a measurable, versioned and reproducible quantity that concentrates in DNA methylation in mammals and separates self-templating codes from sequence echoes; the self-templating memory function is conserved across the tree of life, but the molecule that carries it is lineage-specific.

papers.abstract_full: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and LD Score regression are closely related in practice, yet the quantities used in these approaches have apparently different mathematical definitions. GWAS evaluates the association between a genetic variant and a phenotype, whereas the LD Score of a locus is defined from pairwise correlations among genetic variants. Here, we show that these apparently different quantities can be represented within a common geometric framework.We represent standardized genetic variants as vectors in the sample space and construct a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix from their outer products. Spectral decomposition of this matrix provides a common orthogonal eigenbasis for the genetic variation observed in the sample. Both individual genetic variants and the component of the phenotype contained in the SNP space can be represented using coordinates defined with respect to this same eigenbasis. LD Score and phenotype--genotype association can consequently be expressed as different operations on these common coordinates.We numerically verified these relationships using simulated genotype data containing correlated groups of loci and a phenotype vector constructed from components both within and orthogonal to the SNP space. Direct calculations of LD Score and phenotype--genotype association agreed with their corresponding spectral representations to numerical precision.These results show that GWAS association and LD Score are not quantities defined in unrelated mathematical spaces, but can be viewed as different operations performed within a common coordinate system. We term this representation Genetic Geometry. This framework provides a unified view of GWAS and LD Score regression and provides a basis for investigating why their locus-specific quantities exhibit the relationship exploited by LD Score regression.

papers.abstract_full: Background:  The chromosome 9 CTNNAL1–ELP1 locus is associated with pediatric sepsis susceptibility, but the regulatory gene and developmental context remain unresolved. Methods: We integrated pediatric sepsis fine-mapping (510 cases, 994 controls) with eQTL data from resting and stimulated adult monocytes, neonatal myeloid regulatory data, ELP1 exact-junction splicing, colocalization, and cis-Mendelian randomization using exposure side instruments selected and frozen before outcome extraction. Twenty-eight prespecified gene–state exposures across five regional genes were evaluated. Results: rs28361152 dominated the 11-variant disease credible set (posterior inclusion probability=0.605). ABITRAM showed strong colocalization after 24-hour lipopolysaccharide stimulation (PP.H4=0.904) and supportive sharing after interferon-γ stimulation (PP.H4=0.716), whereas CTNNAL1 regulatory signals were disease-distinct. Higher genetically predicted TMEM245 expression after 24-hour interferon-γ stimulation was associated with lower sepsis susceptibility (odds ratio=0.941, 95% confidence interval 0.908–0.975; P=8.11×10⁻⁴; false-discovery-rate q=0.011). Sensitivity analyses were directionally concordant; however, mediation remained unresolved because colocalization was not evaluable. Neonatal models yielded no purity-qualified credible sets, and rs28361152 was absent from all 11 ELP1 exact-junction credible sets. Conclusion: ABITRAM was the leading disease-linked regulatory candidate, whereas TMEM245 provided secondary Mendelian-randomization support without demonstrated locus mediation. These findings refine the locus into developmentally informed regulatory candidates and therapeutic hypotheses requiring functional validation.

papers.abstract_full: A single nucleotide polymorphism (rs2304297) in the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of  CHRNA6 , encoding the α6 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit, is associated with adolescent smoking behavior. Humanized rats carrying the “C” or “G” allele show sex- and genotype-dependent responses to adolescent nicotine, yet the variant does not alter the protein sequence and the mechanism has remained unknown. We examined the molecular consequences of rs2304297  in vivo in the adolescent ventral tegmental area (VTA).  Chrna6 transcript abundance did not differ by genotype, nor did transcript stability or polyadenylation site selection. The variant was instead associated with a transcriptional signature spanning myelin maintenance (  Enpp6 ), lipid metabolism (  Retsat ), and genomic repair (  Polq ), and with elevated basal lipid peroxidation in α6  GG animals. Computational folding predicted greater conformational flexibility of the “G” allele, and spatial colocalization of  Chrna6 with miRNA-365-5p was reduced in α6  GG animals of both sexes. Coordinated expression of the two transcripts, however, followed a sex-by-genotype pattern, absent in α6  CC females and α6  GG males. These same groups showed elevated tyrosine hydroxylase expression and dopaminergic neuron number, and expansion of the  Chrna6 co-expression network following nicotine. We propose that rs2304297 acts through two distinct layers: genotype determines spatial engagement of miRNA-365-5p with the transcript, while sex determines whether that engagement produces functional regulation. These findings identify a post-transcriptional mechanism for a non-coding nicotine addiction risk variant and demonstrate that its molecular effect can be uniform while its consequences are not.

papers.abstract_full: Background  Across phenotypic and genotypic studies, executive functioning (EF) has been shown to be associated with externalizing behaviors, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), aggression, and substance use, and is a proposed underlying mechanism of these behaviors. However, there is limited research on the shared biological mechanisms underpinning EF and externalizing behaviors, including their overlap at the level of genomic regions. Methods  The current study used genome-wide association study summary statistics of EF, ADHD, aggressive behavior, alcohol use, and alcohol use disorder to examine whether the heritability of these traits or the co-heritability between them is enriched for genes expressed in particular tissues or stratified by other annotation types. Additionally, the study examined the genomic regions contributing to the covariation between EF and the externalizing traits to identify genetic variants and genes that may be underlying their overlap. Results  First, across all phenotypes, there was evidence for enrichment of genetic signals in DNase hypersensitive sites and H3K4me1 regions, and significant enrichment among genes expressed in the anterior cingulate cortex and frontal cortex. Second, when combining results across regional methods, there was evidence for associations between EF and each of the externalizing behaviors in regions on chromosomes 1, 11, and 15. Conclusions  These findings highlight biological pathways that may  link the relations between EF and externalizing behaviors and provides additional evidence of EF as an underlying mechanism of externalizing behavior.

papers.abstract_full: Sequence models predict the molecular effects of genetic variation, yet their contribution to interpreting Alzheimer’s disease (AD) association signals remains uncertain. Here we analysed AlphaGenome Atlas predictions for 111,446 common variants across 75 regions from a European-ancestry genome-wide association study (GWAS) of AD and related dementias. Predicted expression effects modestly tracked association within loci (mean partial Spearman ρ = 0.018,  P = 0.003) and were higher in variants with the highest posterior inclusion probability than in correlated variants outside credible sets (mean difference, 0.044 percentile units;  P = 0.005). This relationship remained after adjustment for genic position (ρ = 0.011,  P = 0.026). Predicted splicing effects also tracked association, but this relationship was attenuated after the adjustment. Expression and splicing scores were associated with the corresponding Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) quantitative trait locus (QTL) status, although these analyses did not establish colocalization or agreement in allelic direction. Across 50 loci with multiple fine-mapping candidates, predicted cellular labels were no more concentrated than in position-matched comparisons, and expression direction profiles showed no detectable excess concordance with lead variants. These findings support expression predictions as complementary evidence for interpreting AD risk variants, while showing that the assignment of cellular context must account for fine-mapping uncertainty.

papers.abstract_full: Background  The inner ear is supplied by the labyrinthine artery, which is functionally close to an end artery with limited collateral reserve. Microvascular abnormalities have been implicated in sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) and age-related hearing loss, yet inner-ear microvasculature cannot be assessed in vivo and current hearing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are underpowered. We evaluated the shared genetic architecture of retinal arteriolar tortuosity (retina_AT) with blood pressure, cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) and hearing phenotypes, and examined whether retinal microvasculature could serve as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature. Methods  We used linkage-disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) to estimate SNP heritability for 19 phenotypes and genome-wide genetic correlations (rg) for 11 prespecified pairs. We ran approximate Bayes-factor colocalization (coloc.abf) between 19 independent retinal loci and systolic blood pressure (SBP), together with 95% credible-set fine-mapping, UCSC gene annotation, colocalization with GTEx aortic and tibial-artery expression QTL (eQTL) data and with white-matter hyperintensities (WMH), hearing-GWAS power calculations, and univariable and multivariable Mendelian randomization (MR) of blood pressure and heart rate on hearing. Results  Only retina_AT with SBP was significant genome-wide (rg = 0.10, P = 4.2×10⁻⁵, FDR q = 0.00042). The strongest retinal locus, 13q34, did not colocalize (PP.H3 = 0.996; peaks about 267 kb apart; allelic heterogeneity), whereas two secondary loci colocalized strongly—CSK at 15q24 (PP.H4 = 0.98; 3/3 credible variants within CSK) and PAWR at 12q21 (PP.H4 = 0.99; 3/5 within PAWR)— supported by tissue-matched, moderate eQTL evidence (PP.H4 = 0.71–0.75). At 13q34, retina_AT with WMH was an adequately powered null (PP.H4 = 0.019; only this region and phenotype were tested). On the hearing side, sharing of the blood-pressure magnitude (rg ≈ 0.10) was a near-powered null (about 1.5-fold larger sample needed for 80% power under that assumption, versus about 15-fold for weak rg ≈ 0.03 sharing), and rg ≥ 0.12 was excluded; MR found no robust causal effect. Conclusions  Retinal arteriolar tortuosity shows limited, distributed genetic sharing with blood pressure at the vascular-tone genes CSK and PAWR; no sharing with WMH was observed at 13q34 (only this region was tested). Retinal microvasculature may serve as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature, but this analogy awaits direct testing by larger, vessel-oriented hearing GWAS and inner-ear tissue functional studies.

papers.abstract_full: Spatial transcriptomics increasingly generates multi-slice atlases spanning developmental, regenerative, and disease-associated states. Identifying genes with spatial pattern remodeling across these states is essential for understanding tissue reorganization and the underlying gene programs, yet few existing methods systematically detect such changes while accounting for variation among replicate slices. Here we introduce DeSPA, a statistical framework that models gene specific spatial variation within each slice using a linear mixed model, tests for cross-state remodeling by aggregating evidence across replicate slices, and organizes identified genes into interpretable spatial co-expression modules that reveal coordinated spatial programs. Simulations show that DeSPA achieves high power while controlling the false discovery rate under inter-slice heterogeneity. In mouse embryogenesis, it recovers programs linked to extracellular matrix organization, muscle formation, neural development, and erythrocyte development. In diabetic testis, it reveals disruption of a late-spermatid spatial program consistent with known spermatogenic dysfunction, while maintaining stable gene rankings under coordinate rotation. In axolotl brain, regeneration preserves a developmental like biosynthetic backbone but reorganizes it into regeneration-specific modules. Across two mouse intracerebral hemorrhage models, DeSPA resolves a conserved spatial injury program alongside model-specific synaptic and tissue-response programs. Together, these findings establish DeSPA as a scalable and interpretable framework for detecting spatial pattern remodeling and resolving coordinated spatial programs across diverse biological states.

papers.abstract_full: PURPOSE: Socioeconomic status has been associated with sleep disturbance; however, the link between annual household income and insomnia symptoms, considering the additive association with work-life balance, has yet to be examined. Therefore, we investigated this association among Japanese female care workers. METHODS: Between 2015 and 2016, 451 women aged 18-60 years who worked in older adult care services were enrolled in this cross-sectional study. Insomnia symptoms were measured using the Athens Insomnia Scale. Categorized annual household income was divided into two categories (high/middle vs. low) based on the median annual household income from the national survey. Work-life balance was assessed by examining work-to-family and family-to-work conflicts. Exposure was defined as a combined category of income and work-life balance. Data were collected via self-administered questionnaires. Prevalence ratios (PRs) of insomnia symptoms were estimated using modified Poisson regression. RESULTS: The multivariable-adjusted PR (95% confidence interval [CI]) of insomnia symptoms was 1.43 (1.01-2.01) in the low- compared with the high/middle-income group. Compared with the group with high/middle income and better work-life balance, the PR (95% CI) of insomnia symptoms was 1.27 (0.80-2.00) among those with low income and better work-life balance. Meanwhile, high PRs were observed for both income groups with a worse work-life balance (2.00 [1.45-2.74] for high/middle income and 3.02 [2.00-4.56] for low income). CONCLUSIONS: Improving work-life balance may help mitigate insomnia symptoms regardless of income, while low income was associated with a higher prevalence of insomnia symptoms.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Background:  The global shortage of nurses has increased the demand for internationally educated nurses (IENs) in the United States. Recruitment agencies play a critical role in facilitating the migration and workforce integration of Spanish-speaking IENs; however, the quality, transparency, and professional support offered by these agencies remain largely unexplored. This study aimed to systematically identify and evaluate international recruitment agencies serving Spanish-speaking IENs seeking employment in the United States. Methods: An environmental scan (E-scan) of international nursing recruitment agencies was conducted using a 7-phase framework, with elements adapted from the PRISMA 2020 statement to guide identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion. The initial search identified 267 agencies across websites and social media; after applying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 20 were included. Agencies were assessed using a dichotomous questionnaire developed for this study and based on International Council of Nurses recommendations, evaluating four dimensions: information access, reliability, professional support, and visual design. Preliminary evidence supported content validity (Aiken’s V = 1.00; three experts), internal consistency was high (KR-20 = 0.90), and inter-rater reliability was near-perfect (Cohen's κ = 0.947). Results: Of the 267 agencies initially identified, 20 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the final review. Considerable heterogeneity was observed among agencies. Interstaff and PRS Global achieved the highest overall quality scores (0.885), followed by Global American Nurses (0.846). These agencies demonstrated consistently high performance in information accessibility, reliability, professional support, and visual design. In contrast, ANP Health and Global Nursing Recruiters obtained the lowest overall scores (0.154), followed by CareerKnacks International (0.269), mainly due to deficiencies in reliability, professional support, and digital platform quality. Visual design represented the strongest-performing dimension among high-quality agencies, whereas reliability was the weakest dimension among lower-ranked agencies. Conclusions: Substantial variability exists in the quality of recruitment agencies serving Spanish-speaking internationally educated nurses seeking employment in the United States. papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is an effective minimally invasive treatment for hepatic hemangioma, but systemic inflammatory response (SIR) syndrome-associated complications should be considered. This study aimed to explore the mechanism and potential targets in SIR caused by RFA of hepatic hemangioma. METHODS: Murine orthotopic hepatic hemangioma model with RFA treatment and heme-stimulated human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVECs) were utilized for investigations. Colocalization staining was conducted to observe mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) oxidation damage and the colocalization of TLR9, MyD88 and TRAF6. Co-IP was conducted to test the interactions among TLR9, TRAF6 and MyD88. Inflammatory cytokines were detected by ELISA. VBIT-4 was utilized to inhibit the release of mtDNA. RESULTS: Along with the SIR caused by RFA, there are mitochondrial swelling and damage, increased release of mtDNA and increased TLR9 expression. Inhibiting mtDNA release using VBIT-4, generation of inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-18, IL-6 and TNF-α significantly reduced and TLR9 expression was reduced. Further rescue experiment by overexpressing TLR9 counteracted the inhibition role of VBIT-4 pretreatment on inflammatory cytokines generation. In hepatic hemangioma mice with RFA treatment, injection of sh-TLR9 could alleviate the development of SIR, manifested as markedly reduced inflammatory cells (lymphocyte, monocyte and neutrophil) and inflammatory cytokines. Mechanistically, TLR9 interacted with MyD88 and TRAF6, and TLR9 silencing attenuated the SIR in association with the changes of Merlin phosphorylation. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrated the involvements of mtDNA/TLR9 mediated inflammatory response in SIR of hepatic hemangioma following RFA. Targeting TLR9 might be an available strategy to prevent SIR in RFA of hepatic hemangioma.

papers.abstract_full: The acquisition of paired appendages was a key innovation in vertebrate evolution. Although HoxA/D paralog groups (PGs) 9-13 play central roles in patterning paired fins and limbs, the evolutionary origin of this paired appendage-patterning system remains unknown. Here, we show that HoxA/D PG9-10 genes are essential for the early establishment of pelvic fin progenitors in zebrafish, and that Hox9-10 function is similarly required for hindlimb progenitor formation in the Iberian ribbed newt. In zebrafish, combined disruption of five HoxA/D PG9-10 genes abolishes the detectable pelvic fin progenitor population, resulting in complete loss of pelvic fins. A Tg(hoxa10b:EGFP) reporter labeled cells in the presumptive pelvic fin field before pelvic fin bud formation. Importantly, simultaneous CRISPR-mediated disruption of all seven Hox9-10 paralogs in the Iberian ribbed newt similarly impaired the establishment of hindlimb progenitors, suggesting that an early requirement for Hox9-10 function in hind appendage development predates the divergence of ray-finned and lobe-finned vertebrates. Together, these findings identify an evolutionarily conserved role for posterior Hox9-10 genes in the initial establishment of hind appendage progenitors. Because overlapping posterior Hox paralog groups are subsequently deployed during paired appendage patterning, this early Hox9-10 requirement provides a developmental link between the posterior axial Hox code and the paired appendage-patterning system. Our results are therefore consistent with the hypothesis that recruitment of a posterior Hox code into hind appendage progenitor formation contributed to the evolutionary assembly of the vertebrate paired appendage-patterning system.

papers.abstract_full: This cross-sectional secondary analysis examined medical rehabilitation use and regional bypass among Korean children and adolescents with registered disabilities, using a two-stage access framework that distinguished entry into medical-institution rehabilitation from out-of-region use after entry. We analyzed public-use data from the 2023 National Survey on Persons with Disabilities, restricting the sample to respondents younger than 19 years (n = 399; weighted national estimate, 88,611). Weighted descriptive statistics and modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors were used to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Overall, 50.0% had no medical-institution rehabilitation use, 31.5% used in-region rehabilitation, and 18.6% used out-of-region rehabilitation; among rehabilitation users, 37.1% reported out-of-region care. In stage 1, non-developmental disability type was associated with higher medical rehabilitation use (PR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.28-2.03), whereas eup/myeon residence was associated with lower use (PR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.46-0.94). In stage 2, province residence (PR, 2.13; 95% CI, 1.38-3.27) and non-developmental disability type (PR, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.13-2.69) were associated with out-of-region use, while male sex was associated with lower out-of-region use (PR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.42-0.92). The most common reason for non-use was use of non-medical facilities (27.4%); better treatment and absence of nearby medical institutions were leading reasons for out-of-region care. Pediatric medical rehabilitation access involves challenges to both non-use and out-of-region use, with implications for local entry support, regional capacity-building, and cross-sector service integration.

papers.abstract_full: Background/Objectives: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) may affect the two eyes asymmetrically, but visual impairment is commonly classified by visual acuity (VA) in the better-seeing eye. We compared interocular-presenting VA differences in unilateral early versus late AMD, assessed the association between late AMD and worse VA in the AMD-affected eye, and compared refractive status between the affected and fellow eyes. Methods: We analyzed 1112 adults aged ≥40 years with unilateral AMD (1049 early and 63 late) from the 2017-2020 Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Interocular VA difference was calculated as the logMAR VA of the AMD-affected eye minus that of the fellow eye. Survey-weighted modified Poisson regression estimated prevalence ratios (PRs), adjusting for age, sex, anisometropia, and the interocular difference in absolute spherical equivalent refraction. Exploratory analyses examined neovascular AMD and geographic atrophy separately, and sensitivity analyses assessed alternative model specifications. Results: Mean interocular differences were -0.004 logMAR (95% confidence interval [CI], -0.016 to 0.008) in early AMD and 0.184 logMAR (95% CI, 0.077 to 0.291) in late AMD. The weighted proportions with VA ≥ 0.2 logMAR worse in the AMD-affected eye were 10.15% and 58.31%, respectively. The adjusted PR for this outcome was 4.95 (95% CI, 3.46-7.09; p < 0.001) for late versus early AMD. Exploratory subtype-specific analyses showed similar associations for neovascular AMD and geographic atrophy. No statistically significant interocular differences in refractive status or astigmatism severity were detected; however, the wide 95% CIs, particularly in the late AMD group, precluded conclusions of equivalence. Conclusions: Unilateral late AMD was associated with greater interocular presenting VA asymmetry than early AMD, and the association remained consistent across sensitivity analyses. However, these cross-sectional findings do not establish longitudinal progression or directly demonstrate implications for spectacle prescribing or binocular visual function.

papers.abstract_full: Background: Oral symptoms and preventive dental-care practices during pregnancy remain insufficiently characterized in Romania. This study described self-reported oral manifestations, oral-hygiene practices, and dental attendance and explored their cross-sectional associations with gingival bleeding, dental pain, and perceived oral-health impact. Methods: This single-center cross-sectional study included 101 pregnant women recruited at the Ginecho Clinic, Craiova, Romania, between October 2025 and July 2026. Participants completed a 21-item electronic questionnaire in the clinic with clarification available from the medical team. Oral conditions were self-reported/perceived rather than clinically diagnosed. Prevalence ratios (PRs) were estimated using Poisson regression with robust variance; multivariable models simultaneously included preventive behaviors, maternal age, parity, and trimester. Results: Gingival bleeding (68.3%), gingival swelling (66.3%), and salivary-flow alterations (57.4%) were frequently reported. Most participants brushed once daily (66.3%), never used interdental cleaning (68.3%), and had not attended a dental visit during pregnancy (81.2%). In adjusted models, brushing at least twice daily was associated with lower prevalence of gingival bleeding (aPR = 0.56; 95% CI: 0.32-0.97) and higher perceived oral-health impact (aPR = 0.47; 95% CI: 0.23-0.99). No preventive behavior was significantly associated with dental pain after simultaneous adjustment. Conclusions: Self-reported oral manifestations were common and preventive practices were limited in this convenience sample. These exploratory associations do not establish temporality or causality and require confirmation in prospective studies using validated instruments and clinical oral examinations.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Adults with activity limitation carry a heavier cardiometabolic burden, but whether differences arise in disease detection or subsequent management remains unclear. Cascade studies rarely measure health-care use directly and compute each stage against all prevalent cases-a cumulative formulation that cannot separate detection from later transitions. I assessed utilization, screening, unmet need, and conditional cascade attainment together. METHODS: I analyzed the ninth Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cycle (2022-2024), a nationally representative cross-sectional survey (16,672 adults aged ≥19 years; cardiometabolic and cascade analyses were restricted to adults aged ≥30, and cancer screening to adults aged ≥40). I estimated prevalence ratios (PRs) using survey-weighted Poisson regression, adjusted for age, sex, education, income, smoking, and drinking, with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery control across 17 comparisons. I defined cascade stages conditionally and, secondarily, cumulatively. RESULTS: Activity limitation (11.0%) was associated with higher prevalence of hypertension (PR 1.10, 95% confidence interval [CI]1.04-1.17) and diabetes (PR 1.23, 95% CI 1.11-1.37). Outpatient (1.75, 1.63-1.88) and inpatient (2.20, 1.95-2.48) utilization were higher, whereas general health (0.99, 0.95-1.02) and cancer (0.99, 0.95-1.03) screening were not. Unmet need was 19.0% versus 7.7% (2.39, 2.10-2.71). Awareness was higher (1.06-1.14), but no statistically detectable differences were observed in conditional treatment (0.98-1.01) or control (0.98-1.17). Cumulative point estimates for treatment were higher (1.06-1.11), retaining the awareness difference. CONCLUSIONS: Higher utilization did not correspond to greater screening or lower unmet need, and higher awareness was not accompanied by statistically detectable advantages in treatment or control. Cumulative and conditional cascades answer different questions; reporting both locates where a management difference arises.

papers.abstract_full: AIMS AND BACKGROUND: Here, we present a simple endodontic imaging procedure that leverages expert extensible markup language (XML) annotations of publicly available periapical radiographs. MATERIALS AND METHODS: To develop a machine-learning model for automated severity classification, this work used a publicly accessible dataset of periapical radiographs with labeled lesions. After building a lesion-level index from XML annotations and aggregating bounding boxes into image-level features, 3,924 radiographs were split into stratified training, validation, and test sets. A weighted residual network (ResNet)-18 model was fine-tuned with a class-balanced loss, achieving optimal performance at the best validation checkpoint. To identify radiographic trends and sources of classification error, model predictions were further examined using confusion metrics, clustering of penultimate embeddings, and visual explanations. RESULTS: Lesion-level analysis identified 6,741 annotated locations across 3,924 radiographs, showing frequent multi-lesion presentations and a predominance of moderate cases. A weighted ResNet-18 model demonstrated middling classification performance, with strong recall for mild lesions but much decreased detection capability for intermediate and severe disease. Interpretability evaluations revealed that the model concentrated on lesion locations for accurate predictions, whereas embedding visualizations and clustering demonstrated that lesion severity resides on a continuum rather than in distinct categories. CONCLUSION: We constructed a weighted ResNet-18 model to identify periapical lesion (PL) severity in three categories using the Mendeley periapical radiograph dataset. Our results imply that the model's deep feature representations exhibit distinct radiographic embedding patterns and a well-organized error structure. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The application of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to two-dimensional periapical and panoramic radiographs (PRs) for diagnosing "Periapical Lesions" with the complexity of anatomical structures and overlapping artifacts in the oral and maxillofacial (OMF) region would be useful for clinicians in diagnosing and predicting oral disease when integrated with routine electronic health records (EHRs).

papers.abstract_full: INTRODUCTION: Lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic decreased disease transmission by reducing social interactions but also potentially hindered access to medical care. For individuals who face social and structural barriers to healthcare, such as people with HIV, the overall effect on medical care is unclear. METHODS: Using data from the RV254/SEARCH010 study, a cohort of people with acutely treated HIV, we examined changes in HIV care during the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants with at least one suppressed viral load measurement (≤1000 copies/mL) after 24 weeks on antiretroviral therapy (ART) between 1 January 2018 and 30 September 2023 were included to assess maintenance of HIV care. Time periods were defined as pre-COVID-19, COVID-19 and post-lockdown. COVID-19 was further divided into lockdown 1 (16 March to 3 May 2020), lockdown 2 (1 May to 6 June 2021) and the open inter-lockdown period. Generalised estimating equations were used to calculate prevalence ratios (PRs) of measurements/year and ORs of viral suppression, with 95% CIs. Analyses were adjusted for demographic factors, ART regimen and enrolment status (newly enrolled or established in care). RESULTS: Among 606 participants, 591 (97.5%) were male with a median age of 26.9 years. Participants had 3.50 measurements/year in the pre-COVID-19 period, which decreased to 2.36/year (aPR 0.67 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.70)) during the COVID-19 period and 2.56/year (aPR 0.73 (0.71-0.75)) in the post-lockdown period. Older participants also had fewer measurements/year compared with those 18-19 years of age (20-29 years, aPR 0.90 (0.82-0.98); ≥30 years, aPR 0.88 (0.80-0.97)), as did sex workers (aPR 0.91 (0.85-0.96)). Viral suppression remained unchanged during the COVID-19 (aOR 0.95 (0.43-2.07)) and post-lockdown (aOR 0.95 (0.48-1.88)) periods compared with pre-COVID-19. During the COVID-19 period, there were fewer measurements in lockdowns 1 and 2 (0.34/year and 0.14/year) than the inter-lockdown period (2.82/year). CONCLUSIONS: Lockdowns during COVID-19 reduced HIV care engagement, particularly among participants established in care, without affecting viral suppression.
