Wheat landraces constitute an invaluable reservoir of adaptive genetic diversity that has evolved through centuries of natural and farmer-mediated selection under resource-limited environments. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the mechanisms underlying environmental resilience in wheat landraces, integrating evidence across physiological, biochemical, hormonal, molecular, ecological, and agronomic scales within a single framework. It examines how coordinated adaptive strategies-including stress escape, avoidance, tolerance, and recovery-interact with root system architecture, rhizosphere processes, plant-microbe associations, and resource-use efficiency to enhance resilience under multiple abiotic stresses. Recent advances in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, pangenomics, and multi-omics integration have substantially improved our understanding of the genetic and molecular basis of environmental adaptation, creating new opportunities for the identification and deployment of resilience-associated traits. The review further discusses how these discoveries are being translated into climate-smart wheat improvement through genome-wide association studies, marker-assisted and genomic selection, speed breeding, gene editing, and artificial intelligence-assisted phenotyping. In addition, sustainable agronomic management, conservation strategies, farmer participation, and policy frameworks are considered as complementary components supporting the effective utilization of wheat landraces. By integrating adaptive biology, modern breeding technologies, sustainable agronomy, and socio-economic perspectives, this review presents a comprehensive framework for conserving and utilizing wheat landrace diversity to accelerate the development of climate-resilient wheat cultivars and strengthen global food and nutritional security under increasingly unpredictable climatic conditions.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Characterizing the protein-protein interactions (PPI’s) enable novel therapeutic strategies and defining precise disease mechanisms for human diseases including cardiovascular space. However, vast gap remains between theoretical PPI’s search space and physically validated data due to the high cost, low throughput, and high false-positive rates. We present an AI-driven, high-performance computing framework to map the human structural interactome and identify novel therapeutic PPIs for cardiovascular diseases. To overcome historical structure-availability and throughput bottlenecks, we combined proteome-wide AI-predicted structures (Published by Innophore) with NVIDIA’s EquiDock, an end-to-end deep learning docking framework. Deployed across 460 NVIDIA’s H100 GPUs, this interaction-aware pipeline evaluated a curated matrix of 3.3 million co-localized protein pairs, successfully reducing rigid docking runtimes from hours to seconds. We calculated binding free energies using PRODIGY and integrated these deep learning-derived PPIs with population-scale GWAS datasets, like CARDIoGRAM and Pan-UK Biobank, to map cardiovascular polygenic networks. The draggability assessment for these novel targets was done using a PocketVec-driven chemogenomic classifier and rDock screening. Cross-referencing our predictions against benchmark interactome repositories (HuRI, BioGRID, STRING, PDBbind) isolated hundreds of thousands of high-confidence, novel physical interactions. Retrospective literature benchmarking confirmed that this computational framework prospectively anticipated subsequent wet-lab discoveries, including TCAP–COLQ and SDHA–IDH2.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the leading cause of birth defects; most critical (c)CHD newborns will develop neurodevelopmental disorders. Abnormal placental development may be involved, as genetics explains only 30% of sporadic CHD cases. Growing evidence suggests that placental dysfunction may result in heart and brain defects, as it shares a common early development. We hypothesized that newborns with critical CHD exhibit sex-specific alterations in placental mitochondrial biogenesis and function which may affect the fetal growth trajectory. Term placenta and paired umbilical cord (UC) blood were collected at birth from cCHD (n=16) and matched control (n=20) neonates. Mitochondrial lipid complex (phosphatidic acid (PA), phosphatidylglycerol (PG), cardiolipin (CL)), acylcarnitine metabolites and organic acids were determined in placenta by LC-MS/MS. Gene expressions of enzymes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics and lipid pathway were measured in placenta by RT-qPCR. Placental protein expressions of β-oxidation and OXPHOS were determined by Western Blot. Mitochondrial dynamics were reduced in cCHD placentas, particularly in male infants. Long-chain acylcarnitine (LC-acar) metabolites decreased in female cCHD placentas and increased in males, while they increased in both sexes in UC plasma. Malonate levels increased in cCHD placentas, affecting the TCA cycle. CL de novo synthesis was dysregulated in the cCHD placentas, though CL concentrations were similar in both groups. The cCHD placenta may compensate for cardiac defect in a potential sex-dependent manner, leading to an accumulation of LC-acylcarnitine in the UC plasma. Placental mitochondrial adaptation to metabolic needs may have a cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Background/Objectives: Noonan syndrome (NS) is characterized by marked phenotypic variability. Although the classical phenotype includes short stature, craniofacial dysmorphism, skeletal abnormalities, and congenital heart defects, some patients present with subtle or atypical manifestations, making clinical recognition challenging. Methods: This retrospective case series included six pediatric patients with molecularly confirmed NS managed at the Department of Endocrinology and Metabolic Diseases, Polish Mother's Memorial Hospital-Research Institute, Lodz, Poland. Medical records were reviewed for auxological data, phenotypic features, endocrine and skeletal assessment, cardiovascular findings, associated conditions, and multidisciplinary management. The aim of this study was to characterize the phenotypic diversity of NS in pediatric endocrine practice, with particular emphasis on growth patterns, endocrine and skeletal manifestations, and atypical clinical presentations. Results: The six patients demonstrated markedly heterogeneous clinical presentations. One boy exhibited the classical phenotype with severe short stature and pulmonary valve stenosis, whereas a girl with typical NS features maintained relatively preserved growth around the 3rd percentile. Another patient presented with progressive resorption of permanent incisor roots and a coexisting pathogenic NBN variant. A boy with LZTR1-associated NS and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) demonstrated a blended phenotype and height between the 25th and 50th percentiles. Two girls lacked characteristic NS dysmorphism and presented predominantly with growth impairment, accompanied by markedly low bone mass in one case and a prolonged diagnostic pathway in the other. GH deficiency was not identified in the evaluated patients, and rhGH therapy was initiated in three patients. Conclusions: NS encompasses a broad clinical spectrum, ranging from classical phenotypes to atypical presentations dominated by growth, skeletal, or dental abnormalities. Neither the absence of characteristic dysmorphism nor relatively preserved growth excludes the diagnosis, while coexisting genetic conditions may further modify the phenotype. Awareness of this heterogeneity is essential for appropriate recognition and individualized multidisciplinary care. In selected children with otherwise unexplained growth or atypical clinical findings, consideration of NS and genetic evaluation may help establish a unifying diagnosis and potentially shorten the diagnostic pathway.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Developmental Systems Cardiology (DSC) conceptualizes congenital heart disease as a lifelong adaptive process shaped by interactions among biological, developmental, psychosocial, environmental, and healthcare systems. As survival has improved, contemporary challenges increasingly include neurodevelopment, psychosocial wellbeing, educational participation, healthcare engagement, and long-term adaptation, requiring multidimensional assessment beyond traditional physiological outcomes. This third article in the DSC series proposes a measurement framework for operationalizing adaptation across the lifespan. Rather than introducing new measurement domains or replacing established assessment recommendations, DSC provides an integrative architecture for linking existing measures across genomics and epigenomics, prenatal exposures, developmental physiology, neurocardiac interactions, family and social determinants, environmental influences, digital phenotyping, and healthcare-system context. Longitudinal measurement serves as a cross-cutting principle for characterizing adaptive trajectories and identifying periods of vulnerability and opportunity. Within this framework, adaptation is a dynamic, measurable process emerging through interactions among individuals, families, healthcare systems, and broader environments. Measurement therefore encompasses developmental functioning, resilience, participation, quality of life, healthcare transitions, and implementation outcomes alongside biological and clinical indicators. Established domain-specific standards, including neurodevelopmental assessment recommendations, can populate this broader architecture. This approach emphasizes integration rather than instrument development, while preserving the specificity and utility of established measures within individual domains. By integrating validated measures across domains, developmental stages, and time, DSC may provide a common language for research, registries, quality improvement, implementation science, and lifespan care. Its proposed contribution lies in organizing multidimensional measurement to better understand how adaptive and maladaptive trajectories emerge and evolve across development.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Duplications of distal 20q are uncommon and the connection to oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum (OAVS) is still not clear. In this paper we describe a family-based cytogenetic case of a geographically isolated community in Northern Italy. Clinical data, pedigree information, and cytogenetic report from the proband were collected. Relatives were examined for OAVS-related features. Subtelomeric FISH analysis was performed with probes for 20qter and D22S1726 using peripheral blood lymphocytes to assess the rearrangement in detail. Descriptive statistics with 95% confidence intervals were computed. FISH demonstrated additional terminal material on der (22) consistent with a complex subtelomeric rearrangement and partial trisomy of 20qter. Among the 30 evaluated relatives, 15 (50.0%; exact 95% CI, 31.3-68.7) carried the rearrangement. Of these, 5 (33.3%; exact 95% CI, 11.8-61.6) exhibited features within the oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, including preauricular tags, microtia or aural atresia, hemi-facial microsomia, ocular anomalies, vertebral defects, congenital heart disease, and hearing impairment. FISH does not provide information about the duplication segment or genes involved; therefore, MYT1 inclusion into the duplication cannot be confirmed and requires further chromosomal microarray, SNP-array, MLPA or genome sequencing analysis. In this pedigree, the findings support the distal 20qter/20q13.33 as a possible candidate genomic region associated with OAVS-related features and support high-resolution genomic studies and genetic counselling in affected families.
